title: Octillion adds 3 GWh of battery capacity in India - electrive.com
content:
Octillion Power Systems has opened its third battery factory in India. The new plant in Gujarat has an annual capacity of more than 3 GWh and will supply battery systems for electric cars, commercial vehicles and buses.
Octillion Power Systems has opened a third battery factory in India.
Image: Octillion Power Systems
The US battery supplier says the new factory in Halol, in the western state of Gujarat, can produce more than 48,000 battery systems per year at full capacity. Together with the company’s two other factories in India, Octillion now has capacity for more than 150,000 battery systems or around 9 GWh per year in the country.
The Halol site covers more than 13,000 square metres. According to Octillion, it took less than eight months to convert the previously empty building into a battery factory. The site is the company’s ninth production facility worldwide.
India wants to localise more of the battery supply chain
Octillion’s expansion comes as India is trying to build up more of the battery value chain domestically. While battery systems are increasingly manufactured in the country, India still depends heavily on imports of lithium, cobalt and nickel. According to research by the International Institute for Sustainable Development cited by Octillion, local content for components such as battery cells, electric motors and controllers remains below 20 per cent for many manufacturers.
The government has introduced several measures to address that dependence. The National Critical Minerals Mission is intended to support domestic exploration and processing, while India has removed customs duties on 25 critical minerals. According to Octillion, the government is also preparing a policy specifically aimed at processing battery minerals.
Octillion says its approach in Halol includes integrating its production processes, thermal modelling and battery management systems with the local supply base. Nikhil Parchure, SVP at Octillion Power Systems, says that simply adding production capacity is not enough.
“A resilient EV supply chain in India can’t just mean more square footage — it means depth: local sourcing, local quality control, and local engineering talent working side by side with our global standards,” said Nikhil Parchure, SVP at Octillion Power Systems. “That’s what we’ve built in Halol. As India moves toward its 2030 electrification targets across cars, trucks, and buses, our customers need a partner who can scale with them without exposing them to global supply chain volatility, and that is exactly the role we intend to play.”
There should certainly be demand for the additional capacity. By 2030, India is targeting EV shares of 30 per cent for private cars, 70 per cent for commercial vehicles and 40 per cent for buses. Among the government programmes supporting the transition are
PM E-DRIVE
on the vehicle side and the Advanced Chemistry Cell Production-Linked Incentive scheme for domestic battery production.

I’m looking forward to connecting with others in the industry, sharing ideas and working through real-world supply chain examples together during the workshop. I’m also excited to hear how other organisations are approaching similar challenges and brainstorm practical solutions.

How is Jabil helping organisations manage disruption with its logistics operating model?
Jabil helps organisations build greater visibility, flexibility and resilience into their logistics operations so they can respond more effectively when conditions change. title: India Lifts Wheat Export Ban to Ease Global Supply
content:
India Lifts Wheat Export Ban to Ease Global Supply
Prioritise Us
on Google
Directorate General of Foreign Trade (DGFT) has confirmed the lifting of the ban on wheat exports effective immediately (Image source: Getty Images/umesh negi)
India has lifted its three-year wheat export ban, easing pressure on global supply as Black Sea shipments face disruption
India has scrapped its years-long ban on wheat exports, a move that could ease global supplies at a time when Black Sea shipments are under renewed strain from escalating attacks between Russia and Ukraine.
The Directorate General of Foreign Trade (DGFT) issued notifications on 24 August 2026 confirming the change took effect immediately. The revised policy covers wheat, the durum variety, flour, maida, semolina, wholemeal atta and resultant atta, all of which move from the prohibited to the free export category.
For senior supply chain leaders in food, agriculture and trade, the decision reopens one of the world's largest wheat producers to global buyers at a moment when established
supply routes are under pressure
India first banned wheat exports in May 2022, citing food security concerns and rising domestic prices linked to disruption from the
Russia-Ukraine war
. The restrictions were extended to wheat flour exports later that year.
“The export policy of Wheat flour and related products falling under the HS Code 11010000 is revised from 'Prohibited' to 'Free' with immediate effect.”
An official regulatory update from Lav Agarwal, Directorate General of Foreign Trade, Indian Government, 24 August 2026
The government eased the policy gradually rather than all at once. In February 2026, it allowed exports of 2.5 million tonnes of wheat and a further 500,000 tonnes of wheat products, citing improved stock availability. This month's decision removes the remaining restrictions entirely.
India's total food grain production reached an all-time high of 376.563 million tonnes in the 2025-26 season, up 5.3% on the previous year, according to government data released in May 2026. Wheat production alone rose to a record 120.657 million tonnes, an increase of 2.712 million tonnes on the prior season.
The US Department of Agriculture is forecasting India's domestic wheat
stockpiles
to end the 2026-27 season at a record level, pointing to a genuine surplus rather than a policy gamble.
India's domestic wheat stockpiles are predicted to end the 2026-27 season at a record level
Why the timing matters
The change lands as global wheat markets face fresh disruption from the Black Sea, the export corridor through which Russia and Ukraine, together among the world's largest wheat exporters, ship the bulk of their grain.
Benchmark Chicago wheat futures climbed more than 17% between the start of July and late August 2026, driven largely by a shortfall in Black Sea supplies. Escalating attacks on commercial vessels and ports in the region have pushed prices to a two-year high.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said over the weekend of 22-23 August 2026 that Russia had rejected a truce offer to end attacks on ships carrying agricultural commodities through the Black Sea.
For import-dependent buyers, the exposure is significant:
Egypt, the world's largest wheat importer, sourced more than 82% of its wheat imports from Russia and Ukraine in the first half of 2026
Indonesia, the second-largest importer, has contracted around 600,000 tonnes from alternative origins for July-September shipment
Algeria, Bangladesh, Jordan, Thailand, Tunisia and Vietnam also rely heavily on Black Sea wheat
Kpler analysis suggests prolonged disruption could push buyers toward strategic purchasing and a shift toward European wheat
India's surplus positions it as a credible alternative origin, alongside Bulgaria, Australia, Romania and Argentina.
What it means for supply chain leaders
A pickup in Indian wheat shipments could ease supply pressure across Asia, Africa and the Middle East, regions with the greatest exposure to Black Sea disruption.
It also reintroduces India as a variable in global grain
sourcing strategies
, three years after the country effectively withdrew from that role. Buyers who built supply chains around alternative origins during the ban may now find India competing for the same contracts as Bulgaria, Australia, Romania and Argentina.
The shift comes even as India itself has emerged as an importer of some other agricultural commodities, a reminder that the country's t
rade position
remains dynamic rather than fixed.

title: Mercedes CEO on his fake-V8 electric AMG: 'like a born-again Christian'
content:
Mercedes-Benz
Mercedes
Mercedes-AMG
Mercedes CLA electric
Fred Lambert
| Aug 25 2026 - 8:38 am PT
Mercedes-Benz CEO Ola Källenius, a self-described “petrol head” who once ran AMG, says driving an electric AMG with a simulated V8 turned him into “a born-again Christian.”
The comments, made in a new interview, are Mercedes’ clearest pitch yet that enthusiasts, not just early adopters, are supposed to love its next wave of EVs.
Källenius made the remarks to
’s James Attwood during a drive of the new C-Class Electric in Finland. The context was the
Mercedes-AMG CLA 45
, whose electric powertrain can simulate a V8 engine down to the pops, bangs, and feedback of virtual gearchanges.
“When I first drove the CLA 45 with that system, I was like a born-again Christian,” Källenius said. “It was the best V8 I’d ever driven: it had all the feeling of a V8 but with more power and torque.”
That is a notable endorsement from someone with Källenius’s résumé. Before becoming Mercedes CEO in 2019, he ran the AMG performance division, oversaw the company’s Formula 1 engine operation in Brixworth, and was executive director of operations at McLaren during the SLR McLaren program.
Selling performance to a skeptical audience
Källenius’s core argument is that the things car enthusiasts obsess over haven’t disappeared with electrification — they’ve just moved.
“For traditional car nuts it feels like you’re learning a new language,” he acknowledged, comparing the shift to arguing about “a 386 or a 486 processor” on a laptop in his university days. “The technology race has always been there as a combination of hardware and software, but now you have that in cars too.”
He’s betting the performance business grows on that basis. “Our intent is to over-proportionally grow the performance side of the business,” Källenius said, adding that AMG is now developing cars on bespoke platforms to maximize performance while still sharing components with the wider Mercedes lineup.
The simulated V8 is central to that plan. Mercedes has leaned into engineered sound across its performance EVs — the
AMG GT electric supercar revealed in May
pairs more than 1,000 hp with the same kind of artificial engine note. It’s a bet several automakers are now making: Hyundai’s Ioniq 5 N and Dodge’s Charger Daytona use similar tricks to give electric performance cars a soundtrack and simulated gear shifts.
A software-defined Mercedes
The interview also underlined how far Mercedes is folding software into its identity. During the drive, the C-Class Electric’s AI assistant interrupted Källenius mid-sentence to volunteer that “the feeling of driving at high speeds on the autobahn can be exhilarating.”
The car runs Mercedes’ MB.OS operating system, which also underpins the new combustion S-Class and C-Class — meaning the software-defined shift isn’t limited to EVs. Mercedes is midway through launching 40 models in three years by the end of 2027, built on new MMA and MB.EA electric architectures that spawned the
CLA and its near-500-mile range
and the new C-Class and GLC.
Källenius framed that pace as only possible through a “thought-through architecture strategy.” As he put it: “If every nut and bolt on every one of those cars was new, you could never do it.”
Still hedging on the timeline
For all the enthusiasm, Källenius was candid about where demand actually is. He said the industry has “turned a corner” on electrification but admitted “the consumer is not quite there yet.”
He also stressed that Mercedes “didn’t wobble” on its long-term goal of going electric-only, while keeping its commitment to “high-tech electrified combustion engines” in the meantime — the same both-powertrains hedge most legacy automakers have adopted after cooling EV demand forced them to slow their timelines.
Asked whether car development might slow down now that electrification is mainstream, Källenius pushed back, quoting company founder Karl Benz: “The love of inventing never dies.”
Electrek’s Take
The headline quote is fun, and Källenius is appears sincere, but it’s worth being clear-eyed about what’s happening here. A “born-again Christian” moment over a fake V8 is, at bottom, an admission that the emotional case for performance EVs still leans on nostalgia for the thing they’re replacing. Hyundai proved with the Ioniq 5 N that simulated shifts and sound genuinely make an electric performance car more engaging to drive, so this works. But in my view, it’s a bridge, not a destination.
Regardless, my stance on the “fake” engine stuff is always: I don’t really care, as long as it is optional.
So far, I think Ferrari’s approach to this is the best, but I’m curious to see how well Mercedes can implement theirs.

title: BMW i3 Touring captured on video for the first time [Video]
content:
Peter Johnson
| Aug 25 2026 - 7:44 am PT
With the sedan version now on sale, the new
BMW i3 Touring
was captured for the first time with its wagon tail on display.
BMW i3 Touring breaks cover ahead of its debut
i3 went on sale
in June as BMW’s second Neue Klasse model, following the iX3 SUV. In Germany, the i3 50 xDrive First Edition model starts at €75,340 ($86,400). The standard model is priced at €65,900 ($75,500).
In the UK, the i3 50 xDrive First Edition is available starting at £57,905 ($76,500), on the road. BMW said the standard version would go on sale this autumn, priced from £53,005 ($70,000), OTR.
At least one more variant will join the lineup. After a preview was shown during the i3s debut, the new Touring was captured for the first time.
Although it’s still covered, you can see in the new video from
CarSpyMedia
that the Touring version has a considerably longer rear end and a sloped roofline that looks more like a wagon than the standard i3 sedan. It’s similar to the
hatchback and fastback models.
The front end is expected to remain the same as the sedan with BMW’s new twin headlights, kidney grille, and redesigned emblem.
Inside, the i3 Touring will share BMW’s Neue Klasse cabin design and infotainment system. The setup includes a 17.9″ floating central infotainment display and a 43″ Panoramic Vision display that spans the base of the windshield.
BMW i3 50 xDrive First Edition interior (Source: BMW)
Based on BMW’s sixth-gen eDrive (Gen6) with a 108.7 kWh battery, the i3 50 xDrive is among Europe’s longest-range EVs with a WLTP range of up to 566 miles (912 km).
While the Tourer variant is expected to offer significantly more interior space, it’s likely to sacrifice some driving range. Like BMW’s other wagon models, it’s also expected to be slightly more expensive.
BMW i3 50 xDrive First Edition (Source: BMW)
On the EPA rating scale, the i3 50 xDrive has an EPA-estimated driving range of around 440 miles on a single charge.
With an 800V architecture, the electric sedan can regain nearly 250 miles (440 km) of range in about 10 minutes at DC fast-charging speeds up to 400 kW. In the US, the 2027 BMW i3 will have a native NACS port.
BMW began i3 production at its Munich plant earlier this month, and deliveries are scheduled to begin this fall. We should learn more about the Touring variant soon.

Micah Toll
| Aug 25 2026 - 7:36 am PT
One of the most common questions I get from readers isn’t just about speed or range anymore. Increasingly, I’m hearing more questions about battery safety.
People see the occasional viral video of an e-bike battery fire and wonder if they should be worried about charging their battery in the garage, apartment, or workshop. The reality is that quality lithium-ion batteries from reputable manufacturers
are remarkably safe
, but when failures do occur, they can be dramatic enough that many riders want an extra layer of protection.
That’s where products like
Yolin’s lithium-ion battery charging cabinet
come in. I recently spent some time testing the cabinet, and while I admittedly wasn’t sure what to expect going in, I came away more impressed than I anticipated.
At first glance, it looks like a fairly ordinary steel workshop cabinet on locking casters. But open the door and you quickly realize it’s been purpose-built for charging lithium-ion batteries.
Workshop model
I tested is the bigger of the two variants and includes a pair of three integrated AC outlets inside the cabinet, making it easy to keep up to six chargers neatly organized instead of having extension cords running everywhere.
Since I was testing mine in my dad’s workshop, I ended up using it for much more than just e-bike batteries. Cordless drill batteries, impact driver packs, power tool batteries – they all found a home inside next to my e-bike batteries. After a while, it basically became our dedicated lithium battery charging station.
There’s also a smaller version that is around half the height and has just three AC outlets inside, which is still probably enough for the casual rider or weekend warrior.
One thing I particularly appreciated was that the cabinet is designed around actual charging workflows instead of simply being a metal box.
Several e-bike batteries fit comfortably on each shelf alongside their chargers, making it practical for anyone managing multiple bikes or tools. I could also see this being a great solution for bike shops, construction companies, landscaping businesses, or delivery fleets that have batteries cycling through chargers all day long.
The feature that gives me the most peace of mind, though, is something you hopefully never need.
Inside the cabinet are automatic fire suppression canisters – small puck-shaped units mounted near the ceiling that are designed to discharge if exposed to the extreme temperatures associated with a battery fire. Combined with the cabinet’s double-wall steel construction, the idea is to help contain a thermal runaway event rather than allowing it to spread immediately throughout a room. Yolin says the cabinet’s design references several European fire-resistance standards and incorporates a containment-focused structure intended to provide up to 90 minutes of fire resistance.
Since the cabinet isn’t exactly cheap
, part of what you’re paying for is the active fire suppression, temperature control, and other smart features that take it beyond just being a sturdy steel box.
Just as useful during everyday operation is the cabinet’s aforementioned thermal management.
A temperature-controlled ventilation fan automatically switches on when additional cooling is needed, helping prevent unnecessary heat buildup while several batteries are charging simultaneously. You can program the maximum temperature you want the cabinet to reach, and the fan will click on as the temperature is reached, and then click off again when the extra air flow sufficiently cools things down. Unlike a fan that’s constantly running, this one only operates when required, keeping noise and dust to a minimum.
There’s also an independent smoke alarm mounted inside the cabinet. While that might seem obvious, it’s a smart inclusion since if something does begin going wrong during charging, you’ll know about it quickly instead of discovering it much later. I know very few of us actually respect the “never leave your e-bike battery charging unattended” warning, unless you pop open a folding chair each time you plug in and watch it like a hawk for 3-6 hours. So having a built-in smoke alarm would be useful in the event that something did kick off while you’re in the other room.
The build quality also exceeded my expectations.
The steel construction feels solid, the shelves inspire confidence even when loaded with several heavy e-bike batteries, and the locking door hardware feels better than consumer-grade. The large model weighs over 90 pounds (41 kg) before batteries are added, giving it a reassuringly substantial feel while the locking casters still make it easy to reposition around a workshop.
Yolin also offers a smaller “Urban” version at a lower cost of $599. Interestingly, both cabinets share essentially the same floor footprint, with the Workshop simply adding more height and additional shelving. That means choosing between them is really a question of vertical storage and charging capacity rather than how much floor space you have available. If you’re charging one or two batteries in an apartment or garage, the smaller cabinet probably makes sense. If you’re like me and tend to accumulate far more e-bikes and battery-powered tools than you ever planned, or if you’re managing multiple e-bikes, the larger Workshop model offers considerably more flexibility.
Final thoughts
Hopefully, you never actually find out whether the fire suppression system works. But I’m glad to know it’s there. I guess that’s the funny thing about products like this. Success means you own it for years and never have an exciting story to tell.
For many riders, this cabinet is probably overkill. If you own one high-quality e-bike and charge it occasionally, following normal charging best practices is likely sufficient, unless you just want that extra peace of mind of a safer battery charging location.
But if you’ve got several e-bike batteries, a workshop full of cordless power tools, an e-bike fleet, or simply want another layer of protection between your lithium-ion batteries and the rest of your garage or home, I can definitely see the appeal.
After spending time testing the larger Workshop model, I was pleasantly surprised by just how thoughtfully designed it is. It doesn’t feel like someone simply repurposed a filing cabinet and called it a battery charger. Instead, it feels purpose-built around the way people actually live and work with lithium-powered equipment every day – and that’s exactly what I want to see in a product that’s designed to make charging batteries a little safer.

title: The cheapest new cars to own in America are THESE retro-styled EVs
content:
A study of 50 new cars found that the compact but stylish Fiat 500e was America’s cheapest car to own and drive, beating out the Honda Civic Hybrid by nearly $1,300 per year.
And the second most affordable EV to own? It’s also from Stellantis.
A recent study Self.Inc looked at the total cost of ownership (TCO) of 50 new cars, the little Fiat 500e showed that the Italians really do know a thing or two about building affordable cars easily beating the next-most-affordable option, the Honda Civic Hybrid, with average annual costs of just $3,557 compared to $4,833 for the Civic.
Self says its study takes into account the average costs for four factors: annual fuel or energy costs, annual maintenance costs, annual insurance costs, and annual fees and taxes – the average of the 50? A stout $6,913 per year (up $451 from Self‘s last such study from 2024). Interestingly, the study found that the hybrid cars it tested were the most affordable to own at $5,734 per year, compared to $6,189 battery electrics and $7,025 for ICE-powered vehicles.
And, if that surprises you, wait until you read this next bit …
Charged up at number 2
The Fiat 500e may not have been too huge of a surprise, given its low entry price, small size, and general efficiency, but if anything is going to convince you that All Lists Are Weird (© Jo Borrás, 2026), it’s this little nugget: the second most affordable EV to own on Self‘s list is the also by Stellantis: the also retro-styled Dodge Freakin’ Charger Daytona.
The study found that the Dodge Charger EV cost “just” $911 for a year’s worth of energy, $1,364 in annual maintenance (almost all of that tires), $1,907 in insurance, and $1,117 for annual taxes and fees for a total annual cost of operation of $5,298 – about $200 less than a Tesla Model 3 or a Hyundai IONIQ 6, and about $200 less than the Honda Accord.
On the opposite end of the spectrum, the Porsche 911 and Audi RS7 topped the list with annual running costs well over $10,000, while the Lucid Air came in as the most expensive EV to own, at $10,049 per year.

title: Tesla raises Cybertruck prices by $5,000 despite abysmal demand
content:
Tesla Cybertruck
Fred Lambert
| Aug 25 2026 - 6:14 am PT
Tesla raised the price of the Cybertruck by $5,000 on Monday night, quietly updating its online configurator without changing a single spec.
The Dual Motor all-wheel drive now starts at $74,990, up from $69,990. And it comes while Tesla is running the Cybertruck line at roughly 10% of its planned capacity.
What actually changed
Tesla updated the Cybertruck configurator on the night of August 24. Two of the three trims went up by $5,000 each.
The Dual Motor AWD climbed from $69,990 to $74,990, a 7.1% jump. The Premium AWD went from $79,990 to $84,990. The Cyberbeast held at $99,990.
None of the specs moved. The Dual Motor still lists 325 miles of range, 7,500 lbs of towing, and a 4.1-second 0-60 mph time. Same truck, $5,000 more.
The increase also narrows the gap between the Premium and the Cyberbeast from $20,000 down to $15,000.
A truck almost nobody is buying
Here’s the problem: Tesla built the Cybertruck line at Gigafactory Texas for up to 250,000 units a year. It’s currently selling less than 20,000 per year.
That’s less than 10% of capacity. Tesla has been
throttling Cybertruck production
to avoid piling up inventory, and it still has roughly 3,000 trucks sitting in US inventory.
Actual demand looks even worse once you strip out Elon Musk’s own companies. In Q4 2025,
SpaceX alone bought 1,279 Cybertrucks
, and Musk-controlled entities took 1,339 of the 7,071 units registered in the US. Without those purchases, Cybertruck registrations would have fallen 51% year-over-year.
For context, Ford sold more F-150 Lightnings than Tesla sold Cybertrucks — and
Ford canceled the Lightning
for not selling enough.
A pricing rollercoaster with no logic
The strangest part is what Tesla’s pricing has done over the past year. The truck launched well above its promised numbers, and it’s been bouncing around ever since.
Tesla briefly sold a single-motor Long Range RWD version at $69,990, then killed it after just 173 sales. In February, it dangled a $59,990 dual-motor AWD variant, told buyers it was “only for the next 10 days,” and pulled it almost immediately.
That same dual-motor truck settled back at $69,990. Now it’s $74,990. That’s a $15,000 swing on essentially the same vehicle in a matter of months.
Electrek’s Take
None of this makes sense. Tesla is running its Cybertruck factory at roughly 10% of capacity because it can’t find enough people who want to buy the truck. The logical response to weak demand is to cut prices, not raise them. Tesla just did the opposite.
And the pricing history makes it worse. This is the same dual-motor Cybertruck that Tesla briefly offered for around $60,000 earlier this year. There was clearly some demand at $60,000. At $70,000, that demand thinned out. At $75,000, with no changes to the truck, it’s hard to see who’s left to buy one.
We don’t know what Tesla is doing here, but it can’t be good.
During an earnings call earlier this year, Musk put aside the idea of shutting down Cybertruck production. He even suggested that Cybertruck could be used commercially for cargo if consumer demand really dried out. It sounded more like someone who didn’t want to admit defeat rather than someone with a plan.

title: Need a panel upgrade for an EV charger? Schneider may have a workaround
content:
EV Charging
EV Chargers
Schneider
Michelle Lewis
| Aug 25 2026 - 5:00 am PT
Schneider Charge. Photo: Schneider Electric
Schneider Electric’s
new 48-amp home EV charger
is designed to solve one of the priciest problems that can come with buying an EV: discovering that your house needs an electrical panel or service upgrade before you can charge at Level 2 speeds.
The new Schneider Charge uses built-in dynamic load management to monitor how much electricity a home is using and automatically turn the EV’s charging rate up or down. That means some homeowners may be able to add a charger without exceeding their home’s existing electrical capacity.
Schneider says panel and service upgrades can cost anywhere from $2,000 to $6,500 or more, depending on the house and the work required.
“As homeowners buy EVs and add high-power electric technologies, many are realizing their existing electrical systems were not built for that level of demand,” said Shawn Bonacorsi, head of electrification solutions at Schneider Electric’s North America operations. “Schneider Charge helps remove that installation hurdle by enabling safe, reliable Level 2 charging within a home’s existing electrical capacity, making EV charging simpler and easier at home where most charging takes place.”
How Schneider Charge manages a home’s electrical load
The charger’s SmartAmp system uses included current transformers – sensors installed around electrical conductors – to measure a home’s electricity use in real time.
If other big electrical loads, such as an electric dryer or oven, start pulling more power, SmartAmp can temporarily reduce the EV’s charging speed. When demand elsewhere in the house drops, it can increase the charging rate again.
The load-management feature keeps working if the home’s wifi goes down, and it doesn’t require a separate monitoring device or gateway.
Schneider Charge can deliver up to 11.5 kW at 48 amps, although the actual charging rate will also depend on the EV’s onboard charger. It comes with a 25-foot cable and a choice of a J1772 or NACS connector.
The initial model is hardwired; Schneider says a plug-in version will arrive in early 2027.
The charger is part of a UL 3141-certified system, which matters because that standard covers power-control equipment designed to prevent electrical systems from being overloaded.
UL Solutions says
these systems can provide a less expensive alternative to panel or utility-service upgrades.
However, whether a managed-load installation can replace an upgrade will depend on the house and whether the local authority having jurisdiction accepts that installation method. An electrician will still need to assess the home’s wiring, panel, service capacity, and local code requirements.
App controls and future grid programs
The Schneider Charge app lets drivers check charging in real time, adjust settings, and schedule charging for times when electricity is cheaper.
The charger also supports OCPP 1.6, an open communications standard used to connect chargers with management platforms. Schneider says that could allow it to support future utility and grid-service programs, although the announcement doesn’t identify any programs available at launch.
Schneider is working with home electrification installer
to provide installation support.
Schneider Charge is now available in the US and Canada through authorized distributors and Schneider Electric’s online marketplace. The company hasn’t yet disclosed the price of the Schneider Charge.

title: E-quipment highlight: 4,400 hp Wabtec FLXDrive electric locomotive
content:
Electric train
e-quipment highlight
Jo Borrás
| Aug 25 2026 - 4:10 am PT
After nearly a year of operation on a dedicated track line at the Jimblebar iron ore mine in Australia, BHP is proving that these 4,400 hp battery-electric powered heavy-haul locomotives are ready for prime time.
Australia’s first brand-new, purpose-built battery-electric locomotives (
) arrived in Port Hedland last November – and the two
Wabtec FLXDrive
BELs were immediately put to the test on BHP’s rail routes between its
Jimblebar
iron ore mines and Port Hedland operations in the Pilbara.
“The Pilbara has always been a place of big ambition, and these locomotives represent the kind of innovation that is needed to keep the region firing,” said Peter Thomas,
Wabtec’s Regional Senior Vice President for ANZ & SEA
. “Wabtec is proud to partner with BHP on this important step toward decarbonising rail operations. These locomotives are purpose-built to perform in one of the world’s most demanding environments, combining advanced battery technology and regenerative braking to deliver high efficiency and lower emissions.”
The train, itself
Wabtec locomotive, via BHP.
While most modern trains use electric drive motors, those are typically powered by diesel engines acting as electrical generators to haul up to 35,000 tonnes of ore. The Wabtec BELs are similarly powered by high-torque electric motors, but in these, the motors draw power exclusively from the locomotive’s batteries – and they are positively MASSIVE batteries!
Each of the Wabtec FLXDrive BELs is weighed down by a 7 MWh battery pack backed by advanced regenerative braking technology that can capture energy during downhill braking and feed it back into the battery.
On some long downhill runs and loaded up with ore, BELs with regenerative brakes could generate enough power to send the unladen train back uphill to get loaded up again, effectively meaning it’ll only need to be charged once,
and then never again
That kind of potential fuel savings is something every mining company will be looking at
– including BHP, who announced plans to add two additional BELs to its Pilbara operations for extended trials just this week:
In FY2026, we commenced commissioning of two purpose-built Wabtec FLXdrive heavy-haul battery-electric locomotives in Port Hedland, marking the beginning of the trial program. Two further locomotives from Progress Rail were delivered to Perth in FY2026 and to be transported to Port Hedland for commissioning and testing in FY2027.
Once locomotives from both original equipment manufacturers are in trial, we expect to be one of the first mining companies globally to conduct side-by-side evaluations of battery-electric heavy haul locomotive technologies from two suppliers within the same operating environment. This creates a unique opportunity to compare [different products] and accelerate learning in large-scale rail applications.
Using gravity to charge up heavily-laden mining vehicles on downhill runs is an idea that’s been put into practice for years
, with great success wherever the topography allows (
since 2017
, at least). Combining that clever use of gravity, traction braking, and battery storage for use on a rail system like this just seems smart, and it makes me think we’re just scratching the surface of all the clever ways electrification and battery storage will eventually get put to use.
I wonder what would happen if you threw some battery electric rail cars into the mix
, as well!? You guys are smart, head down to the comments and let me know.

title: Kepco targets South Korean inverter competitiveness with new tech subsidiary - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
South Korean state utility Kepco has launched a technology-commercialization subsidiary aimed at bringing thousands of its patents to market, with domestic solar-inverter manufacturers among the first industry partners.
Brian Publicover
25 Aug 2026
Applications & Installations
Technology & Products
Inverters
Korea Electric Power Corp. (Kepco) has launched a wholly owned technology-commercialization subsidiary, Kepco Technology Holdings, according to the South Korean Ministry of Climate, Energy and Environment said.
Kepco contributed an initial KRW 20 billion ($14.4 million) in capital and plans to increase cumulative funding to KRW 100 billion over five years through annual KRW 20 billion contributions.
The subsidiary is intended to connect more than 8,000 Kepco patents and other public-sector energy research, including from the Korea Institute of Energy Technology (KENTECH), with startups and energy-technology companies. Its planned activities include technology transfer, direct equity investment, joint-venture formation, and the use of
Kepco’s infrastructure and operational data for demonstration projects
, followed by a scale-up fund for companies as they mature.
Kim Sung-hwan, minister of climate, energy and environment, said the company should serve as a growth platform connecting publicly accumulated technologies with the market and turning corporate ideas into new industries. He added that it could help foster Korean energy “unicorns” and strengthen the country’s position in global energy and green industries.
Three cooperation agreements were signed at the launch. One agreement involved seven domestic solar-inverter manufacturers identified by the ministry as OCI Power, Dass Tech, Dongyang E&P, Ecos, DIK, Geumbi Electronics, and INO ELECTRIC, aimed at strengthening South Korea’s domestic inverter manufacturing base as renewable-energy deployment expands. The agreement centers on cooperation, technology access, and demonstration opportunities rather than confirmed export subsidies, local-content requirements, or a quantified market-share target.
A second agreement, with equipment manufacturers LS Electric, Hyosung Heavy Industries, and HD Hyundai Electric, aims to establish a
direct-current (DC) industrial hub
in Naju, where Kepco is headquartered, covering research and development, investment, demonstration, and commercialization. The agreement remains an early-stage cooperation framework; public reporting does not yet specify project capacity, investment amounts, or construction timelines.
A third agreement established an investment alliance among Kepco, Kepco Technology Holdings, and 10 investment institutions, including the Korea Development Bank and IBK Industrial Bank of Korea, intended to jointly identify promising energy technologies and companies for private investment.
The deals follow a broader push to strengthen South Korea’s domestic energy-technology capacity. Inverter manufacturers formed an industry association in late 2025 to coordinate production and address
cybersecurity concerns
over imported equipment, while Kepco has separately backed large-scale battery storage and grid projects, including a
978 MW/889 MWh grid-stabilization system
completed in 2024 involving several of the same manufacturers now part of the DC-hub agreement.

title: Sharp unveils 11.5 kWh battery for residential use - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
Sharp is launching its Japan-made 11.5 kWh Eee Storage battery, offering 21% more capacity in a 35% smaller footprint, with AI-powered energy management and enhanced whole-home backup capabilities.
Available in Japan from September 8, 2026, the system targets higher solar self-consumption and delivers up to 4.2 kVA during outages, with the battery priced at JPY 3.751 million ($23,550).
Tristan Rayner
25 Aug 2026
Technology & Products
Batteries
Energy Storage
Residential
The Eee Storage JH-WB2621 battery
Sharp has announced a significant update to its premium residential energy solutions portfolio, launching new Japanese-made energy storage equipment with the company’s updated Eee Storage branding.
The new JH-WB2621 model offers an expanded 11.5 kWh capacity via lithium iron phosphate battery chemistry, representing a 21% increase over Sharp’s previous comparable models, while reducing the overall footprint by 35%, making it more compact for urban environments.
Overall, it reduced the volume per kilowatt-hour by 55%, and the product can also be used indoors or outdoors.
The JH-WB2621 has a net weight of 95 kg, with a described “industry-leading lightweight construction” for easier installation, with dimensions of 458 mm x 360 mm x 777 mm.
A central component of the new system is its integration with Sharp’s
Cocoro Energy app and control system
, which now uses AI. The cloud-based system uses AI to learn household living patterns and solar power generation conditions for smart management of battery levels and consumption. According to Sharp, this can raise the solar power self-consumption rate to almost 75%, thereby cutting grid costs.
Sharp Eee Storage specifications
The new battery has a nominal capacity of 11.5 kWh and an initial usable capacity of 10.5 kWh, measured according to Japanese standard JIS C 4413.
The battery has an operating temperature range of -15 C to 45 C. Sharp said installation is possible at temperatures as low as -20 C, although charging and discharging can be significantly restricted at low temperatures to protect the battery. Still, much hotter and colder regions may now be eligible for the new battery.
The storage system can be paired with Sharp’s JH-59TF4 and JH-40TF2 battery-linked power conditioners. One battery can be connected to each power conditioner, with Sharp’s JH-WDT11 battery converter required for each storage unit.
During grid outages, the storage system can supply electricity through the household distribution board rather than requiring appliances to be moved to dedicated emergency sockets. Depending on the system configuration and household wiring, it can also supply 200 V loads such as induction cooktops.
Users can choose between whole-home backup and a configuration in which only selected circuits remain powered during an outage. The latter can extend backup duration by restricting electricity consumption to predefined loads, and may reduce installation costs for homeowners.
Sharp said the new system increases battery discharge output during outages from 3.0 kVA for its previous model to 4.2 kVA, allowing households to run multiple heavy-load appliances simultaneously.
Pricing and availability
New Sharp Eee Storage
The Sharp Eee Storage JH-WB2621 is scheduled for release on September 8, 2026. The company has set initial monthly production volume of 1,000 units for the domestic Japanese market.
Sharp noted the recommended retail price for the 11.5 kWh main battery unit is JPY 3,751,000 with tax ($23,550), with the translated footnote that a “battery-integrated power conditioner, battery converter, multi-energy monitor, etc. are required separately.”

title: Irish electricity generation by grid-scale PV up 51% in 2025 - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
Grid-scale solar farms generated 1.1 GWh of electricity in 2025, 4% of the total and a 51% increase compared with 2024. Electricity storage output from pumped hydro and batteries contributed a small share. Coal fired power plant generation, meanwhile, decreased its share by 52% from 2024.
Blathnaid O’Dea
25 Aug 2026
Applications & Installations
Utility-scale
Half of Ireland’s grid-scale electricity generated in 2025 was from renewable sources, with grid-scale solar farms accounting for 4% of the total, according to newly released statistics from the Central Statistics Office (CSO).
Grid-scale solar farms are increasing their share of the generation burden, providing 1,101 GWh of electricity generation in 2025 – a 51% increase compared with 2024. Grid-scale solar farms
surpassed the 1 GW generation mark
in April 2026, and at the time Irish grid operator EirGrid estimated this was sufficient to meet around 500,000 customers’ power needs.
Grid-scale solar generation reached its
highest all-time peak of 1.26 GW
on 11 August 2026, just before 1 p.m. During that time, solar accounted for around a third of all electricity usage nationally.
Seasonal, daily variations
Summer months tend to have lower electricity supply compared to winter months. Wind generation is higher in winter but during the summer months when wind speeds are lower, solar can step in to generate electricity and supply the grid. According to the CSO’s data, May had the highest amount of solar electricity generation in 2025 with a daily average of 5.66 GWh. Wind’s share was lowest in May 2025, dropping to 22%.
As well as monthly and seasonal fluctuations there was also quite a lot of daily variation in the renewable share.
Ireland recorded its highest renewable generation share in 2025 on 23 Feb. at 86%, while the lowest was recorded a month earlier on 20 Jan. at just 11%.
This daily variability was largely due to differences in wind generation. Wind accounted for 40% of Ireland’s total electricity generation in 2025 and was the largest renewable energy source providing 11,782 GWh of electricity.
In 2025, wind generation increased by 3% compared with 2024, only a marginal increase compared to solar.
Ireland has a major problem with renewables curtailment, wasting enough wind energy to power 667,000 homes in the first half of 2026 alone.
More energy storage capacity must added to the national mix. Ireland has a 10 GW pipeline of storage projects and just under 1 GW of storage capacity connected. According to the CSO’s 2025 generation data, electricity storage output contributed a very small share of electricity grid supply in 2025, at 1%. During periods of high demand, such as from 5 p.m. to 6 p.m., electricity storage, mostly battery discharge and pumped hydro, provided up to 13% of electricity supply. A flexible combination of wind, solar, and storage is required to keep decarbonizing Ireland’s electricity supply.
Non-renewables decline
In 2025, gas remained the largest energy source for electricity generation, accounting for 47% of the total. It generated 13,918 GWh of electricity, which was a 1% decrease compared with 2024’s 14,036 GWh.
More promisingly, electricity generation from coal fired power stations dropped by 52% in 2025 compared with 2024. Ireland
shut down its last coal plant
in June 2025.
Across all sources, electricity generation was 29,335 GWh in 2025, a small increase over 2024’s total of 29,267 GWh. Ireland continued to import a lot of its electricity and net imports increased by more than 1 GWh compared to 2024, reaching 6,130 GWh in 2025. This made up 17% of grid supply.
Orla McCarthy, Senior Statistician in the Climate and Energy Division, CSO, pointed out that the data does not include all supply from what she termed “auto producers who generate electricity primarily for their own use, for example generation from rooftop solar panels.” This means grid-scale solar coupled with domestic solar output is not actually quantified in the data and solar’s share in Ireland’s system is larger than the grid-scale data represented in the CSO’s release.

title: Portugal’s largest solar plant enters administration amid low output, falling power prices - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Welink Energy Portugal 2 UK, owner of Portugal’s 220 MW Solara4 solar plant, entered administration after weak generation, low wholesale power prices, technical issues and rising costs strained revenues and cash flow. The plant remains operational as administrators seek performance improvements and a potential sale.
Pilar Sánchez Molina
25 Aug 2026
Markets & Policy
Utility-scale
Welink Energy Portugal 2 UK Limited, the UK-based company that controls the Solara4 photovoltaic plant in Alcoutim, southern Portugal, has entered administration after lower-than-expected generation, depressed wholesale electricity prices, and technical issues affected the project’s revenue and cash flow.
The special-purpose vehicle, owned by British renewable energy developer Welink Energy, entered administration on 11 June 2026, according to a
document
filed with the UK’s official Companies House register.
The 220 MW facility has been operational since 2021 and was Portugal’s largest solar plant when it entered operation.
According to a report cited by Portuguese media, Solara4 has consistently generated less electricity than initially forecast. The difficulties have coincided with a significant expansion of solar capacity across the Iberian electricity market, contributing to lower wholesale power prices during periods of high solar generation and putting further pressure on the project’s revenues.
Solara4 was developed as one of Portugal’s first large-scale solar projects without a guaranteed regulated tariff, leaving its business model more exposed to wholesale electricity market conditions. The project consists of 661,500 solar modules spread across approximately 320 hectares of non-contiguous land. Its original design envisaged annual electricity generation of around 382 GWh.
In addition to market pressures, technical issues and fires have resulted in periods of downtime and higher maintenance costs. The plant is also involved in a legal dispute with China Triumph International Engineering (CTIEC), which was responsible for its construction. In proceedings before the High Court last July, CTIEC claimed £17.2 million (€20 million) from the WeLink group over outstanding debts related to solar projects.
The project also has exposure of around €64 million involving Investec and Kommunalkredit Austria, which have been identified as its principal creditors.
The insolvency proceedings do not necessarily mean that the plant will cease operations. The stated objective is to improve the asset’s operational performance and prepare it for a potential sale to new investors.
Management of the project has shifted from Welink Investments to Exus. Exus, together with Enertis, is expected to assess the investment required to restore and increase the plant’s electricity generation.
The project’s future could also include hybridization with wind generation and battery energy storage. The wind component, however, remains subject to a decision by the Portuguese Environment Agency.
Solara4’s insolvency has also prompted debate over the conditions under which large-scale solar projects were developed in Portugal.
Some social media users have linked the case to Portugal’s 2019 solar auctions, which produced record-low bids, including a price of €14.76/MWh. However, that comparison does not directly apply to Solara4, which was developed as a merchant project rather than under a subsidized or guaranteed tariff.
João Galamba, Portugal’s former secretary of state for energy, has rejected the connection with the auctions. In a social media post, he instead pointed to delays in the project’s administrative procedures, saying that a licensing process had started in 2023.

title: Residential PV can trigger rebound effects under South Korea’s tiered electricity tariffs - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
Research finds households in South Korea moving into lower tariff tiers after installing PV systems can offset 11% to 22% of expected energy savings, while net metering can further amplify the rebound effect.
Patrick Jowett
25 Aug 2026
Markets & Policy
Research & Development
Highlights
Residential
South Korea
Seoul, South Korea
South Korea’s tiered electricity pricing system can lead to a
rebound effect
following residential solar adoption, according to new research.
Researchers Jiyoung Eum and Gyeong-Seok Choi, from the Korea Institute of Civil Engineering and Building Technology in Goyang, explored whether installing residential solar systems can lead to households in South Korea using more electricity after adopting solar, a phenomenon known as the rebound effect, which occurs when the expected benefits of a more resource-efficient technology are partly offset by changes in consumer behavior or energy use.
In residential solar, for example, households may consume more electricity after installing PV because their self-generated power effectively lowers the cost of consumption. This, in turn, can partially offset the energy-saving and emissions-reduction benefits initially expected from the installation.
Eum and Choi built a simulation framework that matches hourly solar generation against household electricity use to calculate self-consumption rates. It also tracked how households respond when solar adoption shifts them into cheaper price tiers under Korea’s progressive tariff.
Their results found the rebound effect is concentrated in households that cross a tariff tier, with these households offsetting between 11-22% of expected energy savings. In contrast, households that stayed within the same tier saw virtually no rebound effect.
Eum told
pv magazine
the findings show that PV clearly reduces household electricity use and bills but part of the expected savings can be offset as households increase their consumption.
“Under Korea’s progressive tariff, our study finds that this offset is concentrated in households whose consumption falls into a lower tariff tier after installing PV,” Eum said. “These are simulation-based estimates, and verifying them with metered household data would be a useful extension.”
Additional findings from the research paper found households miss annual emission reductions of 19 to 120 kg of CO2 depending on how many months they spend in transition between tariffs, leading to the suggestion that policymakers evaluating residential solar programs should no longer assume uniform decarbonization outcomes.
The research paper also explores the rebound effect in the context of South Korea’s net metering mechanism, finding that net metering amplifies rather than removes the rebound.
Analysis from the research paper says the rebound effect of high-consumption households effectively doubles, from 4.5% to about 9%, under net metering, as these households are likely to drop their grid consumption and therefore cross into a cheaper tier.
The paper concludes that Korea’s progressive electricity tariff can generate potential rebound effects that partially offset intended energy and emissions savings, uncovering “a dynamic that existing policy evaluation frameworks have not accounted for.” As a result, it recommends that rebound adjustment factors differentiated by tier-transition status, system capacity and net-metering eligibility should be incorporated into PV policy evaluation frameworks.
Eum also explained that government support remains an important driver of residential PV in South Korea, with national subsidy programs reducing the upfront installation cost.
Some local governments adds further support, Eum continued, meaning the level and availability of the support can differ by region and from year to year.
When asked what incentives or policies could help support South Korea’s residential PV market, Eum said continued support for reducing the upfront cost is key to sustaining deployment.
“Solar PV incentives and electricity tariff design are also worth considering together, since the tariff structure affects both household bill savings and the rebound that follows,” the scientist added.
The research findings are presented in the paper “
Rebound effects of residential PV adoption under progressive electricity tariffs in South Korea
, available in the journal
Energy and Buildings.

title: Sweden could face 150,000 metric tons of end-of-life panels annually - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Sweden decommissioned just 17 metric tons (MT) of solar panels in 2021, but a new industry roadmap warns that figure could reach 150,000 MT per year by around 2060, and says current recycling and reuse systems are not yet equipped to handle it.
Brian Publicover
25 Aug 2026
Markets & Policy
recycling
Sweden’s annual volume of decommissioned solar panels could grow from 17 MT in 2021 to as much as 150,000 MT by around 2060, according to a new circular-economy roadmap published by Axfoundation, KTH Royal Institute of Technology, and industry partners including Svea Solar, El-Kretsen, Stena Recycling, and REMONDIS.
The roadmap, developed through the CircSolar project and financed in part by Vinnova, Sweden’s innovation agency, draws on scenario modeling by RISE Research Institutes of Sweden. Depending on the pace of solar deployment and how much of the fleet is repowered – replaced with newer panels before reaching the end of its technical life – RISE estimates annual decommissioning volumes could range from 40,000 MT in a lower-deployment scenario to 150,000 MT in a rapid-expansion scenario by 2060, with larger volumes beginning to emerge from around 2035.
“This roadmap is not the end point, but a starting point for collective action,” said Johanna Olofsson Behrman, project manager for future materials at Axfoundation. “By bringing together actors from across the value chain, CircSolar has shown that circular solutions for solar panels require system innovation, shared responsibility and practical collaboration. The next step is to turn these recommendations into action.”
A typical panel weighs about 20 kg and consists of roughly 67% glass, 16% aluminum, 11% plastic, 4% silicon, and small amounts of metals including silver and copper, according to the roadmap. RISE estimates that
dedicated PV recycling infrastructure
would need a recurring annual inflow of around 10,000 metric tons to become economically viable – a volume Sweden has not yet approached.
The roadmap warns that panels currently removed from service are often
handled together with general electronic waste
, which limits opportunities for reuse and specialized recycling. Research led by KTH found that many panels taken out of service are still functional or repairable rather than genuinely at the end of their life.
“After years of exploring what a circular solar power system could look like in practice, we see this roadmap as an important step toward making the transition more tangible,” said Beatriz Pérez Horno, a KTH researcher and one of the roadmap’s authors. “It highlights the opportunities and barriers across the solar value chain and, importantly, helps identify where knowledge, collaboration and action are still needed to turn ambitions into circular and resource-efficient solar systems.”
Under the European Union’s
WEEE Directive
, member states must collect either 65% of the average weight of electrical equipment placed on their market over the preceding three years, or 85% of the WEEE generated domestically. Separately collected PV panels are subject to specific treatment targets of 85% recovery and 80% preparation for reuse and recycling by weight. Only six of 12 European countries reporting PV-specific treatment data met the 85% recovery target in 2021, according to the European Environment Agency.
The roadmap sets out five priority areas: circular design and responsible production, safer handling and transport of panels, extending the usable life of installed systems, higher-value material recovery, and stronger governance and data-sharing across the value chain. Proposed actions include establishing a dedicated PV waste category under the WEEE Directive, developing standardized testing and certification for second-life panels, and creating a national database tracking installed, decommissioned, and planned solar capacity.
“As the industry’s leading actor, we initiated this roadmap because we see both a responsibility and an opportunity to help shape a more circular future,” said Mattias Ringqvist, CEO of Svea Solar. “Extending the lifetime of solar panels and ensuring they are handled responsibly at end of life must become a natural part of how this industry grows.”
Similar challenges are expected elsewhere in Europe as larger volumes of PV modules reach end of life. The European Commission’s Joint Research Centre estimates the EU could accumulate between 21 million MT and 35 million MT of cumulative photovoltaic waste by 2050, with global volumes potentially reaching 60 million MT to 80 million MT over the same period.
Some recyclers are already working to improve recovery economics. A pilot process using
electrohydraulic shockwave fragmentation
has recovered more than 99.5% of a panel’s original weight in testing, including pathways for silicon and silver recovery, while separate
EU-funded projects
have developed dedicated recycling lines for silicon-based modules.

title: Silver prices rebound as AI, data centers add to industrial demand - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Silver prices have resumed their upward trend amid a broader precious-metals rally, while the market heads toward a sixth consecutive annual structural deficit. Growing demand from AI, data centers and electrification is emerging alongside photovoltaics as an increasingly important driver of silver consumption.
Emiliano Bellini
25 Aug 2026
Markets & Policy
After falling to $55.5 per ounce (oz) in mid-July, their lowest level since early December, silver prices began trending upward in early August, reaching $68.3/oz on Aug. 25.
Silver’s recent gains have coincided with a broader rally in precious metals. Gold rose from around $4,000/oz in late July to more than $4,600/oz in late August, supported by geopolitical and fiscal uncertainty, lower bond yields and increased safe-haven demand.
“We remain positive towards gold and silver prices, for both late 2026 and into 2027,” Philip Newman, Managing Director of independent research consultancy Metals Focus, told
pv magazine
. “This partly reflects our expectation that the US Fed will not raise interest rates this year, which in turn will attract increased institutional investor interest. As such, gold could reclaim the $5,000 level and silver $80 before year-end.”
According to Michael DiRienzo, president and CEO of the Silver Institute, the silver market remains “fluid” as the industry heads toward its sixth consecutive annual structural deficit. He expects the shortfall to reach nearly 50 million oz this year.
DiRienzo also explained rising demand from sectors beyond photovoltaics is contributing to silver consumption, pointing in particular to artificial intelligence (AI), data centers, electric vehicles and broader electrification trends. “AI, data centers, electric vehicles and the electrification of everything are supporting demand,” he told
pv magazine
. “The green revolution continues, but AI and data centers are emerging as important sources of demand that weren’t on the map a few years ago.”
Silver is used in AI and data centers primarily as an electrical and electronic material. Key applications include electrical contacts, connectors, switches, relays, circuit boards, semiconductor packaging and power-management equipment. Data centers also require large amounts of electrical infrastructure such as switchgear, power distribution units, backup-power systems and cooling equipment, some of which contains silver-bearing components.
Over the past 12 months, silver prices have experienced an exceptionally volatile rally. Prices rose from around $45/oz in September 2025 to $70–75/oz toward year-end, before surging to an all-time high above $120/oz in late January. The rally then reversed sharply, with prices falling below $80/oz in early February and then reaching around $57/oz in late June.
Silver is a critical mineral for the solar industry and rising prices have put pressure on the PV module market to curb its use. In September, research found the global solar industry could account for
40% of global silver demand

title: A closer look at CATL Tener S 6.017 MWh BESS - pv magazine Global
content: Chinese battery giant CATL is expanding the footprint of its battery energy storage system (BESS) solutions, quietly securing major project deals even for its less heavily marketed products. As ESS News reported in mid-August, CATL has supplied its Tener S BESS to at least two major developers. In May, Grenergy announced a deal for 252 Tener S units, totaling 1.5 GWh, for its Oviedo and Escuderos projects in Spain. The third stage of Quinbrook’s massive Supernode project in Australia will also use the Tener S. Neither announcement, nor a subsequent CATL press release, provided sufficient detail about the Tener S and its two-hour duration to establish the product’s full specifications. The Tener S has not received the same high-profile launch treatment as the Tener Stack or the company’s more recent sodium-ion products. Official datasheet specifications obtained by ESS News now provide a clearer picture of the Tener S and its evolution from CATL’s earlier products. While the EnerC remains listed in the company’s product portfolio, the Tener S represents a significant step up from the 3.72 MWh EnerC, designed for one-hour storage, and the later EnerC Plus, a 4.073 MWh system designed for two-hour applications. Adding some complexity, CATL documentation and brochures refer to the product as both Tener S and EnerS, reflecting changes in the company’s product lineup and naming conventions. Specifications The official specification sheet confirms that the CATL Tener S, also referred to as EnerS, is a liquid-cooled, DC-connected system with 6.017 MWh of rated energy capacity. It achieves that capacity within a standard 20-foot container footprint and weighs 45 metric tons. By comparison, the original EnerC has a rated capacity of 3.72 MWh and weighs 36 metric tons, while the EnerC Plus has a rated capacity of 4.073 MWh. The Tener S operates at 1,500 V and has a typical charge and discharge rate of up to 0.5P. CATL also lists zero degradation, an IP55 enclosure rating and an operating temperature range of -35 C to 55 C among the system’s specifications. At 0.5P, the system’s 6.017 MWh capacity corresponds to approximately 3.01 MW of power for a two-hour configuration. In a four-hour configuration at 0.25P, the corresponding power rating would be approximately 1.5 MW. title: Oman seeks consultants for renewable energy feasibility study - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
A tender in Oman is searching for a techno-economic consultant to complete a feasibility study on renewable energy projects in the governorate of Musandam. The deadline for applications is September 24.
Patrick Jowett
25 Aug 2026
Markets & Policy
Asia-Pacific
Oman’s Nama Power and Water Procurement Company (PWP) has kicked off a consultancy tender for a feasibility study in the northern governorate of Musandam.

title: Greece introduces new spatial planning rules for PV - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Greece has introduced a new spatial planning framework for renewable energy and storage, tightening siting rules for PV and expanding protected areas. The rules cap PV land use at 1.5% in each of 74 regional units but exempt permitted projects.
Ilias Tsagas
25 Aug 2026
Markets & Policy
Utility-scale
Greece’s Ministry of Environment and Energy has introduced a new spatial planning regime for renewable energy and energy storage, including photovoltaic systems.
The new framework has now become state law and has overhauled the country’s spatial planning framework for renewable energy, updating policies dating back to 2008. The previous framework did not include spatial planning rules for energy storage, so the ministry has also introduced provisions covering storage systems.
The new regulations “modernize siting rules by establishing stricter and clearer criteria, restrictions, and guidelines for the installation of new renewable energy plants and storage facilities,” the ministry said in a press release.
The rules also “take into account current environmental, social, and economic conditions and are geared towards the long-term goal of achieving the country’s energy targets by 2050,” it added.
For PV plants specifically, the new siting rules prohibit systems in areas considered “environmentally, culturally and spatially sensitive,” according to the ministry. These include forests land, national park, designated natural monuments and forests of aesthetic value, as well as cultural heritage protection areas, areas designated in Greece as “landscapes of particular natural beauty, beaches used for swimming, protected areas within the Natura 2000 network, wetland sites, and other protected areas.
Many of these restrictions also applied under Greece’s previous spatial planning framework, but the government said the latest update significantly expands the list of protected areas.
More significantly, the new framework sets an upper limit on land use for new PV parks. Greece is divided into 74 regional units, with PV facilities permitted to cover up to 1.5% of the land in each unit.
The ministry said the measure is designed to prevent an overconcentration of projects in specific areas, limit visual and environmental impacts, protect fertile land and local economies, and ensure more balanced and equitable renewable energy development across the country.
The new framework does not apply to projects already under development that have obtained all required environmental permits. It also excludes rooftop PV and small-scale PV plants that do not require licensing.
The regulations also do not apply to large hydropower plants, pumped hydro energy storage projects or green hydrogen production facilities.
The new spatial planning regime is not expected to significantly alter PV investment plans before 2030, as many large-scale solar projects have already obtained their environmental permits and are therefore exempt from the new rules. The framework is, however, expected to have a greater impact on Greece’s PV sector after 2030.
Greece had installed about 11.5 GW of PV capacity by the end of 2025
. The country’s National Energy and Climate Plan targets 13.5 GW of installed PV capacity by 2030 and 35 GW by 2050. Greece is expected to reach its 2030 target this year.

title: Underwater US robot pulls itself from the ocean without human help
content: A US ocean-technology company has recently unveiled footage showing that its autonomous underwater robot can find its surface vessel and recover itself from the open ocean without human intervention.Impossible Metals’ Eureka II autonomous underwater vehicle (AUV) accomplished the recovery in an offshore demonstration in Halifax, Nova Scotia. The California firm unveiled footage of the test on Tuesday, August 25.The smart robot spotted its surface vessel, navigated toward it, aligned itself, and attached to it with an integrated SmartHook system. It then returned to the deck on its own, all without human control. Jason Gilham, Impossible Metals chief technology officer shared that autonomous recovery could make underwater robots easier to use for commercial operations. “Autonomous recovery is a gating function,” Gilham shared. “If a subsea platform cannot reliably retrieve itself in real ocean conditions, outside a lab, it cannot scale.”Finding its way backRecovering autonomous underwater vehicles could be challenging, particularly in open water. Waves, currents, and the movement of the recovery vessel make the process even more difficult.That’s why Eureka II relied on several technologies during the return journey. The first was acoustic positioning to locate its surface vessel while beneath the wave zone. It then switched to computer vision for more precise navigation during the final approach.The Eureka II SmartHook technology.Credit: Impossible Metals / ScreenshotImpossible Metals revealed that the vehicle had AprilTag visual markers on its top plate to guide the recovery. Once in position, a mechanical SmartHook connected to the vehicle and secured it. The system then retrieved Eureka II from the water and returned it to the vessel.According to the company, the entire process was autonomous, with no operator controlling the robot at any point. “Halifax shows it working in open water, and it shows it working the way it will have to work every day in the field,” Gilham said.Cheaper subsea operationsEureka II is a large autonomous underwater vehicle that can operate at depths of up to 19,685 feet (6,000 meters). The robot measures 10.5 feet (3.2 meters) long, 6.4 feet (1.95 meters) wide, and 6.3 feet (1.93 meters) tall. It weighs approximately 8,710 pounds (3,950 kilograms) on land, and carries a 14.4-kilowatt-hour (kWh) battery. The vehicle also features three sets of robotic arms designed to collect mineral nodules from the seafloor.The technology could greatly cut the cost of underwater operations. Traditional recovery often requires crews to step in. This takes time, labor, and further puts personnel at risk at sea. In contrast, a smart robot that can recover itself could be deployed more often with less downtime.Impossible Metals argued that the achievement comes as global interest in critical minerals, subsea infrastructure, and ocean data continues to grow. Environmental concerns are becoming more important for ocean operations.Steve Curnutte, Impossible Metals executive chairman, stressed that the future of ocean technology will depend on greater autonomy and precision. This would let companies do more and reduce their environmental impact. “That is the standard we are building to, and it is how responsible access to the ocean should be earned,” Curnutte concluded in a press release.

title: Robot inspired by Mexican jumping beans moves without batteries
content: Researchers have developed an unusual robot inspired by the unpredictable movements of Mexican jumping beans.Called BeanBot, the device moves without motors, batteries, electronics, or onboard computing, relying instead on its interaction with the surrounding environment. Its motion can vary dramatically depending on the surface and conditions it encounters, allowing it to hop, roll, flip, or slide in unexpected ways.The researchers say the robot demonstrates a new form of movement driven by simple physical interactions, offering insights into how machines could navigate complex environments without conventional control systems.Heat-powered robotResearchers at the Italian Institute of Technology’s Bioinspired Soft Robotics department have developed BeanBot, which is a small robot that can jump, roll, flip, slide and climb slopes without motors, batteries, sensors or a computer. The robot was inspired by the Mexican jumping bean, whose unusual movements come from a moth larva living inside a seed pod. Instead of copying the animal directly, the researchers combined its heat-driven movement with the shape of the bean’s shell to create a robot that can move in several different ways.Bean-Bot is built from two main parts: a tiny heat-responsive spring and a lightweight, bean-shaped shell. The spring is made from a shape-memory alloy (SMA), a material that changes its shape when heated. Magnets hold the spring in place while it stores energy. When the spring gets hot enough, it suddenly releases that energy, pushing the robot off the ground and sending it into the air. The shell then determines what happens next.The robot does not have a system that tells it when to jump, roll, or flip. Instead, its body shape and the surface beneath it decide how it moves. The shell has one curved side and two flat sides, giving Bean-Bot different ways to interact with the ground. The curved side allows it to roll, while the flat sides help it stay stable and can allow it to climb an incline. The shape also helps the robot turn itself over after landing, allowing it to jump again even if it lands in a different position.This simple design gives Bean-Bot a surprisingly wide range of movement. Researchers found that it can jump as high as about 30 centimetres, roll distances of around 80 centimetres, slide across smooth surfaces and flip through the air or after hitting the ground. It can also climb slopes between 10 and 18 degrees when its magnetic force is adjusted. These movements are produced by the same heat-powered spring rather than separate motors or mechanisms.Robot harnesses surfacesThe robot’s movements can also change depending on the surface it lands on. On a smooth surface, a jump may send it mostly upward or cause it to slide. A rougher surface can make it roll, while irregular ground can change the direction and height of its jump. In tests of 92 jumps, about 81.5 percent developed into additional movements such as rolling, sliding, bouncing, or flipping after the initial jump. This means the robot’s surroundings effectively become part of its movement system.Bean-Bot is also extremely simple compared with conventional robots. Its shell weighs about 3.8 grams, while the jumping module is about 8 grams. The complete system uses a 3D-printed shell, an SMA spring and magnets, with no onboard electronics needed to control its movements.There are limits to the design. The SMA spring currently needs temperatures of about 70–80°C to trigger a jump, and the robot can take 30 to 180 seconds to activate and around 130 to 140 seconds to recover before another cycle. The researchers say future improvements to the materials could make Bean-Bot respond at lower temperatures and move more quickly.The researchers see Bean-Bot as an example of a different approach to robotics, where a robot’s body can do some of the work normally handled by sensors, computers and software. Instead of programming every movement, they designed the robot so that its shape, materials and surroundings naturally produce different behaviours.
