title: The Electric Land Rover Defender Just Got Delayed By Two Years: Report
content:
The Electric Land Rover Defender Just Got Delayed By Two Years: Report
The U.S. will get a version co-developed with Jeep's parent company, Stellantis.
- The next-generation Land Rover Defender won't arrive until the early 2030s, per a new report.
- JLR is delaying its rollout to see how the EV market evolves.
- The new Defender will ride on a dedicated BEV platform.
Jaguar Land Rover is delaying the next-generation Defender by two years amid rocky EV demand in its largest market, the U.S., and a steady decline in sales in China, according to The Times of London.
The iconic luxury off-roader is currently available only with combustion engines and is JLR’s best-selling vehicle. It was poised to enter the electric era with a major redesign, but that transition is now not expected to happen until the early 2030s.
The British luxury automaker is navigating a perfect storm across its major markets. The Trump administration’s tariffs on European car imports have squeezed its bottom line, while Chinese automakers continue to eat into its market share. JLR also suffered a costly Russian cyberattack this year that forced the automaker to shut down production for five weeks.
Land Rover Range Rover GT: Interior Reveal
Its global sales in the first quarter of fiscal year 2027, which is the period from April through June 2026, fell 9.2% to 79,300 vehicles. The Range Rover, Range Rover Sport, and Defender accounted for 81% of those volumes, which shows just how important JLR’s three luxury SUVs are to its business.
Still, JLR is attempting to get back in the game with a string of new all-electric models in the pipeline. They include the Range Rover Electric, Range Rover Sport Electric, Range Rover GT and the Jaguar Type 01. The Range Rover Electric was first announced in October 2021 and was originally supposed to launch by 2024, but it too has been delayed by more than two years.
Now, because of the Trump administration’s tariffs—and the fact that the current Defender is built in Slovakia—the next-generation model will reportedly be offered in two versions: one tailored for Europe and another co-developed with Stellantis for the U.S., according to Automotive News.
The electric Defender will ride on JLR’s EV-native platform, the Electrified Modular Architecture (EMA), and a hybrid version is also expected to use the same architecture. The platform underpins the upcoming Range Rover GT, which we saw during a press trip to England in July. That means the new Defender could benefit from the advantages of an architecture designed specifically for EVs, including better packaging, more frequent software updates and an 800-volt electrical architecture.
Range Rover Sport Electric (Prototype)
The U.S. version would reportedly occupy a different segment from the current Defender. The Stellantis partnership could also help JLR reduce its tariff burden. The automaker currently faces a 10% duty on vehicles imported from the U.K. and a 15% duty on those imported from the European Union.
Exactly what Stellantis hardware JLR could use remains unclear. One possibility is a body-on-frame platform such as the architecture underpinning the Jeep Wrangler. Another is Stellantis’ STLA Large EV platform, which underpins the Jeep Recon.
Neither option has been confirmed, so for now, consider them possibilities rather than a preview of what’s actually coming. But all of this shows just how dramatically tariffs, rocky EV demand and Chinese competition are forcing even one of the world’s oldest and most iconic nameplates—the Defender—to rethink its future.

title: Tesla's FSD Lite Seems To Have A Hard Time Seeing Trees And Logs
content:
Tesla's FSD Lite Seems To Have A Hard Time Seeing Trees And Logs
Two different users on X posted videos of their cars failing to see downed trees in the middle of the road.
- On X, two drivers posted videos of FSD Lite v14.1 not stopping for objects in the road, namely fallen trees and wooden logs.
- FSD Lite is designed to run on Tesla's Hardware 3, which has significantly less computing power compared to Hardware 4 used in later cars.
- FSD Lite was introduced this June.
As Tesla tries to scale up its fleet of self-driving cars and roll out the steering wheel-free Cybercab, Full Self-Driving (Supervised) continues to stumble in serious ways.
One video posted on X on August 21 shows a user named Baldersonmichae using FSD on the road at night. Ahead of him, there’s a fallen tree in the middle of the road, but the car doesn’t seem to notice the large mess of branches and leaves and does not slow down. The driver intervenes and manually stops the car to avoid a collision.
This apparently wasn’t a one-off, either. The driver says he tried the same exact spot three more times, all with the same result. Further down in the comments, another Tesla owner posted a video that purports to show his FSD-equipped car hitting a big log at 32 mph without stopping.
Both drivers say they were running what’s known as FSD v14.1 Lite. This new version of the software is specifically designed to run on cars that use Tesla’s Hardware 3 system. Hardware 3 was introduced in 2019 and doesn’t offer the same performance as the Hardware 4 setup of computers and cameras that landed in cars post-2023. The cameras are lower-resolution 1.2 megapixel ones (compared to the 5 megapixel ones on the updated version). Also, notably, the system has significantly less RAM, only 8 GB worth, compared to the 16 GB per chip in Hardware 4.
Earlier this year, Tesla CEO Elon Musk laid out limitations of Hardware 3, saying on an earnings call that the system won't be able to handle true self-driving capability whenever that launches to consumer vehicles.
Tesla pitched FSD Lite as a way to bring the capability of Hardware 4 vehicles to Teslas with lower-performance hardware. But there have been snags. It’s not hard to search online and see complaints about FSD Lite. Complaints range from overheating FSD hardware to vehicles that aren’t tracking correctly in the lane.
Now, it’s a great thing that the driver who had the run-in with the downed tree was paying attention to the road and stopped in time. There’s a reason why it’s called Full Self-Driving (Supervised), folks. Pay attention to the road.

title: Polestar Still Has No Idea Why The U.S. Kicked It Out
content:
Polestar Still Has No Idea Why The U.S. Kicked It Out
The automaker was stripped off its authorization to sell cars in the U.S. model year 2027 onward.
- Polestar said the Department of Commerce has not yet explained its ban on selling cars in the U.S.
- It is arguing that Volvo was granted authorization to sell an EV with an identical software stack.
- The automaker has not appealed the Trump administration's decision.
Polestar has yet to get an explanation from the U.S. Department of Commerce for its decision to effectively force the automaker out of the American car market. The government denied the automaker, which is owned by China’s Geely Group, authorization to sell cars in the U.S. for model year 2027 onward. Its corporate cousin, Volvo, was granted a special authorization to continue selling its cars in the U.S.
In a letter sent to dealers and viewed by The Wall Street Journal (paywall), Polestar said it has yet to hear back from the Trump administration on why it must stop selling EVs in America. The automaker argued that its Polestar 3 electric SUV is mechanically identical to the Volvo EX90, and that both are assembled on the same production line at the Volvo Cars plant in Ridgeville, South Carolina.
Gallery: Polestar 3
At the core of all this is the Connected Vehicle rule, which restricts vehicles linked to hardware or software from foreign adversaries such as China and Russia from being sold in the U.S. The rule was finalized by the Biden administration and argues that vehicles connected to Chinese technology, including telematics and advanced driver assistance systems, could pose a national security risk or potentially be used to spy on Americans.
“In essence, we are currently focusing on getting the attention of (the Commerce Department) to obtain the requested information and to understand the underlying basis for the denial,” Peter Wexler, Polestar’s U.S. head of government affairs, said in the letter viewed by The WSJ. He added that the Volvo EX90 was “a car that is essentially the same as the Polestar 3 and that uses the same software stack.”
The saga took a bizarre twist earlier this month when a New Jersey Polestar dealer filed a lawsuit against the Swedish automaker, claiming that it was planning its U.S. exit for two years and used the government ruling as a cover up. The dealership, Prestige Imports, said Polestar violated New Jersey’s Franchise Practices Act, which generally prohibits automakers from terminating a franchise without at least 60 days advance written notice and good cause.
Sweden's Minister for Foreign Trade Benjamin Dousa said that he worked very closely with Volvo to make sure it met the Connected Vehicle Rule requirements to continue selling cars in the U.S., but Polestar didn't ask for the same help, per Automotive News.
All told, Polestar did not appeal the U.S. government’s ban and instead said it would double down on the European market, which accounts for 80% of its global sales.
That said, if you’re looking for a bargain EV, you may still want to consider a Polestar. The automaker is offering a whopping $25,000 discount on the Polestar 4 coupe and Polestar 3 SUV as it prepares to wind down its U.S. operations. It’s a rather unusual way to end a chapter in the American market. Sell the cars for less while waiting for the government to explain why you can’t sell them at all.

title: The Mercedes CLA 350 4Matic Destroys EPA-Rated Range With Shocking Efficiency
content:
The new Mercedes EV went close to 400 miles in a recent 70 mph range test.
Photo by:
Mack Hogan/InsideEVs
5:35pm ET
The Mercedes-Benz CLA is the company's smallest and lowest-priced EV in North America.
In a 70 mph range test, the four-door car blew way past its EPA-rated range of 312 miles.
It managed to eke out 4.44 miles per kilowatt-hour from its 85-kWh pack.
Mercedes-Benz's littlest EV is actually one of its most impressive. The new
2027 Mercedes CLA-Class
sedan absolutely crushed its EPA-rated range in Tom Moloughney's latest 70 mph highway range test by going 385 miles between fill-ups.
The CLA packs a decently big battery for being the smallest electric Merc on sale in North America: 85 kWh. But it isn't just the big battery that gives the Mercedes such an impressive range. It's also quite efficient. At the end of Moloughney's test for his State of Charge YouTube channel, he saw an average of 4.44 miles per kilowatt-hour. That's far beyond what it's supposed to be capable of.
According to the
, the all-wheel drive Mercedes CLA 350 4Matic has 312 miles of range, considerably less than the single-motor rear-wheel drive model's 374-mile range. Since Moloughney's test car was an all-wheel drive 4Matic model, it beat what the EPA says it can do by a whopping 73 miles—and did it all on the highway at 70 mph. Moloughney isn't alone, either, as
Car and Driver's
75 mph highway test saw 340 miles.
It wasn't like he did anything to give the Merc a boost, either, like messing with tire pressures or driving in especially good conditions. He filled the tires to Mercedes' recommendations and did the test in the summer on the New Jersey Turnpike. If anything, the Turnpike's horrific road surface, with its tire-destroying craters and loads of potholes patches, should be a detriment to an EV's range.
Photo by: Mack Hogan/InsideEVs
Also interesting is that the CLA's efficiency didn't really drop off as the battery depleted. For the first 95 miles, it was averaging 4.50 mi/kWh. For the next 100 miles, it actually improved to 4.52 mi/kWh. The next 95 miles were at 4.46, and then it finished the final 95 miles at 4.44. Mercedes poured a ton of effort into the CLA's efficiency, like using silicone carbide inverters and a two-speed gearbox. Fortunately for the Germans, that effort seems to have paid off. The CLA is a seriously efficient EV, up there with some of the most energy-sipping cars.
Lucid Air
has proven to get around 5.0 mi/kWh, and the Tesla Model 3 has managed 4.6 mi/kWh in
' testing. But the little Merc has is now among the most efficient EVs on the market and comes in at a relatively affordable price, with the 350 4Matic starting at $51,950. Considering the luxury and range you get, I'd say that's a pretty good value.

title: Xiaomi Unveils Custom Chip For Driver-Assist Features
content:
Xiaomi revealed new powerful in-house chips this week that will power everything from cell phones to electric cars.
Photo by:
4:37pm ET
Xiaomi has unveiled its first in-house chips dedicated to AI and self-driving.
The automaker currently relies on Nvidia for its hardware, though that could change as early as next year.
This makes Xiaomi the latest Chinese automaker to ditch U.S.-sourced chips in favor of self-produced silicon.
Xiaomi's next move in cars is happening somewhere you'll never see it: buried deep inside the dashboard, under a heatsink, doing the ungodly amount of math required advanced driver-assistance features.
On Monday, Xiaomi
unveiled
a family of in-house silicon, including the Xring D100 chip designed for "intelligent driving." This makes Xiaomi the latest EV maker investing in home-grown AI inference rather than relying on a market cornered by Nvidia.
Photo by: Xiaomi
Xiaomi's
EVs have historically relied on Nvidia's hardware, beginning with the older Drive Orin system and now the
Drive Thor
. That decision locked the Chinese brand in with the American GPU producer at a time when the entire world is looking at the same company for chips to power the insatiable appetite for AI.
Designing chips in-house comes with a few potential upsides. The D100 could be a buffer against soaring AI chip costs. It means
gets to tune its hardware to its own sensor, software, and driving models. It also means that Xiaomi gets more control over cost, supply, and development timing.
Other Chinese automakers like BYD, Nio, Xpeng have begun exploring in-house silicon development too. This is extremely important as key players in the U.S. AI arms race, like Anthropic's
Dario Amodei,
call for stricter export control of AI compute. Here in the States, Rivian recently announced a custom chip for advanced driving features that is debuting in the R2. Tesla has been designing its own chips to run Full Self-Driving (Supervised) for years.
Let's nerd out on the Xiaomi silicon's specs for a moment.
The D100 packs a 20-core CPU and a 16-core NPU. Xiaomi says that this is the first chip build in mainland China on a 3-nanometer chip production process (meaning it can potentially offer more efficiency and processing density in a single chip). It also supports up to 160 gigabytes of unified memory—enough to run up to a 200-billion-parameter model directly on the device.
For comparison, Nvidia's current Thor hardware is offered with a 14-core, 4-nanometer processor and up to 128GB of memory. Tesla's current Hardware 4 offers 16GB of memory on a single chip and is built on a 7nm process. Its upcoming Hardware 5 is targeting an even more efficient 2nm manufacturing process and is expected to feature up to 144GB of memory.
It's important to point out that it is possible for a system to offer more compute capacity but have lower overall performance due to optimization of overall efficiency. It's not clear if that's the case with Xiaomi's hardware compared to Nvidia or, say, Tesla, because Xiaomi has yet to reveal the system's actual Trillions of Operations Per Second (TOPS), which is a key measurement of speed and performance in AI inference.
Stay informed with our newsletter every weekday
Xiaomi says that it's poured more than $3 billion into the development of its new hardware. That might seem like an expensive way to avoid buying another company's chips, but Xiaomi's top brass clearly believe the independence outweighs the R&D costs.
That figure includes the Xring D100, as well as its O100 AI acceleration chip and O3 System-on-Chip (SoC) platform meant for mobile devices. The O3 is slated to debut in Xiaomi's upcoming 18 Fold cell phone, and the D100 and O100 are planned for commercial applications starting next year.

title: More EV Owners Can Now Get Paid To Power California’s Grid
content:
More EV Owners Can Now Get Paid To Power California’s Grid
The new Chevy Bolt EV and Kia EV9 are among a bunch of new EVs capable of vehicle-to-grid power sharing.
- The West Coast's largest utility is expanding its vehicle-to-everything bidirectional charging program.
- Owners of many new all-electric models can now participate, including those who own the Volvo EX90 and the Chevy Bolt.
- PG&E's initiative allows EV drivers to lower their energy bills and support the grid.
More electric vehicle owners in California can now use their cars’ batteries to share electricity with the grid and get paid for doing it.
Pacific Gas & Electric said Monday that it is expanding its vehicle-to-everything (V2X) program to include EVs from Nissan, Volvo, Polestar and Kia, along with more General Motors models like the Chevy Bolt.
EVs are essentially giant power banks on wheels. They can not only swallow huge amounts of electricity at charging stations, but many can also send that stored energy back to power appliances, homes, and even the electric grid. That capability could be a game-changer at scale, helping reduce strain on the grid during periods of high demand while giving EV owners another source of backup power during outages and natural disasters.
Volvo EX90 charging from a Level 2 home charger.
PG&E said it is partnering with software company Bidirectional Energy, which operates a platform that connects EVs to homes and the grid and allows customers to earn money by sharing power. The utility is also teaming up with renewable energy company PowerFlex to expand V2X adoption across California.
Several GM EVs were already compatible with the program, including the Chevrolet Silverado EV and Equinox EV.
"This expansion is all about choice," David Almeida, the director of clean energy transportation at PG&E said in a statement. "By broadening the mix of eligible vehicles and chargers, we're helping our customers access this valuable technology, while also offering them a way to turn their EV into a home backup and a grid asset."
PG&E said the expanded program now includes the new Chevy Bolt EV, Cadillac Celestiq, Escalade IQL, Nissan Leaf (previous gen), Volvo EX90, Polestar 3, and Kia EV9 and EV6. The Ford F-150 Lightning and Tesla Cybertruck were already compatible with the program.
Residential customers can receive incentives of up to $2,500 for installation, with that amount rising to $3,000 for customers in disadvantaged communities. There’s also a separate $1,500 Early Adopter incentive for the first 250 customers.
For businesses, the incentive is worth up to $4,500, increasing to $5,000 for those in disadvantaged communities. The enrollment period runs through June 2027.
Of course, V2X isn’t quite as simple as plugging an EV into the wall and telling it to start making money. You need specialized hardware to send electricity from the vehicle back to your home or the grid.
A Tesla Cybertruck, for example, can send power to the grid using Tesla’s Universal Wall Connector home Level 2 charger combined with its Powershare Gateway system. GM EVs can use the company’s PowerShift charger, while the Kia EV9 and EV6 can send power to the grid using Wallbox Quasar 2 chargers. PG&E has a full list of compatible vehicles and chargers.
So how much can customers actually earn by sending electricity back to the grid?
One of the biggest advantages of this kind of arrangement is the ability to charge an EV when electricity is cheap, typically overnight, and then send power back to the grid when electricity prices are higher during peak daytime hours. Customers may not necessarily see a big difference in their bank account right away, but they can reduce how much electricity they need to buy from the grid, lowering their home energy bill in the process.
If the value of the electricity exported from the EV exceeds the cost of the energy being consumed by the home, that’s when the savings can turn into actual earnings.
PG&E’s hourly electricity rates change every day and are influenced by factors including transmission costs, grid demand, time of day and weather conditions. According to the utility's Home Flex pricing chart, customers could earn anywhere from 5 cents to 50 cents per kilowatt-hour on August 23.
Right now, V2X still involves a somewhat messy combination of software platforms, compatible vehicles, and specialized chargers. And it's still limited to pilot programs around the country such as PG&E's, which as been running for a couple of years. So the expansion is a welcome step toward making bidirectional charging more useful to a much larger pool of EV owners.

title: Wawa Branded EV Chargers Are Here Thanks To Electrify America
content:
This is what happens when a charging giant and a gas/sandwich giant team up.
Photo by:
Electrify America
12:58pm ET
Wawa-branded
EV chargers
are coming. As a South New Jersey resident, this is very exciting news. While there are already plenty of Wawas with EV chargers, the brands vary and it's kind of hit and miss, as they aren't always the kind of charger or speed you need. For example, the majority of Wawa charging stations near me are Tesla Superchargers, and only one of them allows non-Tesla vehicles. So while that's helpful, it isn't helpful for everyone. However, that's going to change in the coming years, as Wawa just partnered with
Electrify America
to put its own branded chargers at its gas stations.
This partnership is part of
Electrify America's White Label
program, that supplies third-party brands with an EV charging network that the brands customize. In this case, Wawa designs the look of the chargers, the experience, and even comes up with its own pricing. Electrify America builds the network and handles things like maintenance and customer support. So when you pull up to a Wawa charger, it will feel like its own thing, not just an EA charger at a Wawa, which is cool. Wawa also usually has the cheapest gas near me, so I'm hoping it carries its typical values onto EV juice. Also, Wawa, if you're listening, it'd be cool to see a price per kWh on the big digital gas signs.
Photo by: RivianTrackr
To start, eight Pennsylvania locations will get Wawa-branded chargers. Five of which will have have NACS and CCS ports with up 400 kW, while the other three will CCS-only and support up to 350 kW. The 400 kW locations in Upper Darby, Phoenixville, Media, Williamsport, and Reading will each have two chargers capable of juicing up two cars at a time. While the 350 kW Bristol, Allentown, and Quakertown spots will have four single-car charging stations.
At the moment, Wawa has 280 chargers across the 14 different states it operates in. Since Pennsylvania is its home turf, that's where these new chargers will go first, but it should start expanding outward in the coming years.
“This move to testing Wawa branded chargers demonstrates our ongoing commitment to meeting our customers’ fueling needs — whether they require electric charging or traditional liquid fuels," said Rich Makin, Wawa's senior vice president and chief fuel and development officer. By owning Wawa branded chargers, we are always striving to deliver a more seamless, reliable, and consistent experience and this allows us to provide more options throughout 14 states for our customers.”
I shouldn't be excited about anything that comes from the Philly area (eww Birds, go Giants), but I can't help but have love for Wawa. Every road trip must start with a Wawa run, with a few more coffee stops sprinkled in between, depending on how long the road trip is. Now, that'll be the case for more and more EV customers, too.

title: 超43GWh，亿纬锂能等5企储能项目签约、开工、投产
content:
集邦光储观察获悉，近期，亿纬锂能、紫创光科、金麟汇科、金鑫新能、星空钠电等多家企业接连传来项目签约、开工、投产等动态，覆盖储能电池、光伏逆变器及光储产业配套设备、圆柱锂电池、钠离子电芯等领域。
亿纬锂能马来西亚储能电池工厂开工
据中建集团消息，8月24日，近日，马来西亚亿纬锂能三期工厂项目开工。项目位于马来西亚居林东鑫工业园，总建筑面积约20万平方米，由中建三局承建。
据悉，该项目规划年产38GWh储能电池，主要建设电芯厂、化成车间、锂锰工厂、锂亚工厂和动力站、变电站、消防中心等配套用房。项目建成后，将扩充海外储能产能，完善亿纬全球化产业布局。
一光伏逆变器/光储配套项目即将投产
8月25日，据“眉山发布”消息，近日，四川丹棱经开区紫创光科(眉山)智慧能源科技有限公司光伏逆变器及光储产业配套设备智能产线项目即将投产。
据悉，光伏逆变器及光储产业配套设备智能产线项目总投资1亿元，目前已完成厂房修建、设备进场调试等关键工作，各项筹备工作有序收尾，预计今年9月正式投产，投产后可实现规模化量产。
3GWh圆柱锂离子电池项目开工
8月21日，新疆金麟汇科能源科技有限公司年产3GWh圆柱型锂离子电池项目在兵团第十一师（建工师）新型建材经济技术开发区正式开工。
据悉，项目一期总投资3.6亿元。三元体系规划产能2GWh，磷酸铁锂体系规划产能1GWh，产品矩阵覆盖18650、21700及32140三种主流圆柱规格。其中，磷酸铁锂系列聚焦源网侧储能、户用及工商业户外电源等高安全、长循环需求领域。
2.2GWh钠离子电芯项目二期即将投产
据“陇东报”消息，日前，甘肃省庆阳市正宁县石墨烯钠离子电芯项目二期首批生产设备已全部进场到位，整体工程预计9月建成投产。
该由金鑫新能投资、中钠储能新能源科技（甘肃）有限公司具体实施。据悉，该项目总投资10亿元，于2023年3月开工建设，分两期有序推进。
一期工程投资1.8亿元，建设年产3GWh储能生产线、1GWh锂电池生产线，已于2024年顺利竣工投产。二期工程计划总投资8.2亿元，新建2.2GWh石墨烯钠离子电芯生产线，目前已进入施工攻坚关键阶段。
星空钠电钠电池项目落地
据“星空钠电”消息，近日，星空钠电与浙江湖州南浔经济开发区举行钠离子电池智能工厂项目签约仪式。
资料显示，星空钠电成立于2018年1月24日，总部位于辽宁省鞍山市高新区，是一家高新技术企业，隶属辽宁宏成集团，专注于钠离子电池材料研发、储能技术开发及电池生产。

title: 32亿！盛新锂能拟在津巴布韦、尼日利亚建硫酸锂项目
content:
集邦光储观察获悉，8月24日，盛新锂能公告称，公司拟分别在津巴布韦和尼日利亚投资建设年产7.5万吨硫酸锂项目，两个项目计划总投资合计约4.76亿美元（约合人民币32亿元）。
其中，津巴布韦项目计划总投资约2.44亿美元，尼日利亚项目计划总投资约2.33亿美元，建设周期均为19个月。
津巴布韦项目拟由公司全资孙公司Max Mind Investments(Zimbabwe)实施，建设地点位于津巴布韦马尼卡兰省布赫拉区，规划年产7.5万吨硫酸锂。
尼日利亚项目拟由公司全资孙公司Chengxin Lithium(Nigeria)International实施，建设地点位于尼日利亚夸拉州伊洛林，规划年产7.5万吨硫酸锂。
此次拟新增两项海外硫酸锂项目，将与盛新锂能现有海外锂资源布局相衔接。目前，公司在津巴布韦已拥有萨比星锂钽矿，原矿生产规模99万吨/年，可生产锂精矿约29万吨/年；在尼日利亚则正在建设选矿产能50万吨/年的选矿厂，并计划继续扩大产能。公司表示，建设硫酸锂项目主要是为了利用当地锂矿资源，推进原料就地加工，同时降低生产及物流成本。
财报显示，2026年上半年，受锂盐产品销量及销售均价上涨影响，盛新锂能实现营业收入73.58亿元，同比增长355.94%；归属于上市公司股东的净利润10.12亿元，同比增长220.30%。其中，公司锂产品收入73.58亿元，占营业收入99.99%，锂产品毛利率为31.75%。
目前，公司位于印尼的盛拓锂盐项目已实现达产，销售和盈利情况良好。该项目已建成6万吨/年锂盐产能，公司表示将继续借助其产能释放提升海外锂产品供应能力。

title: 超4.8GWh，华为、易事特等3企披露储能订单新进展
content:
集邦光储观察获悉，近期，多家储能企业传来订单新动态，华为数字能源、易事特、常德昆宇接连披露储能订单最新进展，包含大型储能项目推进、并网落地，及钠离子电池订单等。
华为推进埃及4GWh储能项目进展
8月23日，据外媒“DAILY NEWS”报道，埃及电力与可再生能源部与华为举行会议，审查一项本地制造电池储能系统项目的进展，项目总装机容量4GWh。
该项目涵盖储能电站建设与本地化制造布局，计划建设总装机容量为4GWh的多座独立的BESS电站。本次项目将以埃镑计价落地实施，并同步推进储能电池本地化生产布局。
易事特供货800MWh独立储能项目
8月24日，易事特储能宣布，位于新疆和田地区民丰县的立新能源民丰200MW/800MWh独立储能项目，近期已完成反送电并具备并网送电条件。
易事特为该项目提供构网型6.7MW/26.8MWh集中式液冷储能系统。易事特构网型储能系统支持真构网功能，系统支持300%10s有功、无功、视在全过载能力，并具备并网、离网、黑启动等多种运行模式。
常德昆宇获30MWh钠电储能订单
据常德经开区报道，近期，常德昆宇新能源科技有限公司一批由墨西哥客户定制的30MWh储能项目电池，正在加紧生产，预计10月底前完成交付。
据悉，该笔订单金额达3500万元。常德昆宇表示，目前，公司的钠离子产品已销往德国、挪威、荷兰、新加坡等地。预计在2027年年底前，公司的钠离子电池所占销售额比例，将从目前的5%提升到30%以上。
此外，常德昆宇表示，随着全球AI技术发展，人工智能数据中心（AIDC）对储能装置的安全性、循环寿命和倍率性能提出更高要求，而钠离子电池在上述方面具备相对优势，公司将结合AIDC扩张趋势，加快相关产品的推广应用。

title: 国轩高科/远东股份等5家储能企业发布2026年上半年业绩
content:
集邦光储观察获悉，近期，国轩高科、远东股份、思格新能源、艾罗能源、科力远等储能企业相继发布2026年上半年业绩情况，多家企业储能业务实现较快增长。
8月24日，国轩高科发布了2026年半年度报告。报告期内，国轩高科聚焦新能源汽车动力电池与储能电池两大核心主业，业绩实现大幅增长。
2026年上半年，公司实现营业收入277.76亿元，较上年同期增长43.22%；归母净利润达13.86亿元，同比增长278.05%；扣非净利润为1.07亿元，同比增长46.71%。
其中，公司储能电池系统业务在2026年上半年实现营收36.89亿元，占公司总营业收入的13.28%。在精益生产与成本管控的推动下，该业务板块毛利率达到19.50%，较上年同期小幅提升0.15%。
目前，国轩高科已构建起涵盖网源侧、电网侧、工商业、户用及移动储能的全链条产品体系。
报告期内，公司持续深耕储能系统核心技术攻关，不断丰富多化学体系产品矩阵，正式发布了“钠晨”钠离子电池以及“干元智储2.0”储能系统等多款重磅新产品。
在巩固大储市场的同时，公司积极开拓ToC终端赛道，其Gendome系列便携式储能产品在海外市场获得良好口碑，为业务增长开辟了全新市场。此外，公司还推出了定制化的零碳解决方案，持续赋能多场景的绿色低碳升级。
8月21日，远东股份披露2026年半年度报告。上半年，公司实现营业收入129.92亿元，同比增长0.12%；归母净利润2.05亿元，同比增长43.13%；扣非净利润1.99亿元，同比增长73.35%。
其中，储能业务增长较为明显。报告期内，储能业务实现收入4.88亿元，同比增长394.55%，获超千万订单22.31亿元，同比增长421.69%。
项目方面，上半年公司落地河北武强200MW/800MWh独立储能电站、新疆立诺200MW/800MWh构网型独立储能项目，以及拉脱维亚5MW/10MWh储能项目。同时，公司继续拓展海外市场，在南欧市场基础上，进一步布局美国算力储能项目，并稳步拓展欧美、中东等区域。
8月24日晚，思格新能源披露2026年半年度业绩。上半年，公司实现营业收入98.74亿元，同比增长261.2%；期内利润24.28亿元，同比增长201%；经调整净利润24.85亿元，同比增长135.8%。
其中，光储系列产品仍是其主要收入来源，2026年上半年该项业务实现收入92.96亿元，同比增长267.1%，占公司总收入的94.2%。公司表示，收入增长主要来自业务规模扩大及产品销量增加。同时，受原材料成本上升以及加大渠道激励力度影响，该业务毛利率由52.4%降至40.7%。
目前，思格新能源产品覆盖户用、工商及地面电站等应用场景，包括SigenStor、SigenStack及SigenTerra等光储产品。报告期内，公司南通智能能源中心启动运营，并计划根据市场需求、产品结构及产能爬坡情况提升生产和交付能力。
海外市场方面，公司表示将继续深化欧洲市场，同时扩大亚太、非洲及北美市场业务，并探索拉丁美洲、中东及中亚等市场。
艾罗能源2026年上半年实现营业收入31.54亿元，同比增长74.59%；归属于上市公司股东的净利润亏损3513.21万元，同比下降124.78%；归属于上市公司股东的扣除非经常性损益的净利润亏损4840.08万元，同比减少146.14%。
在储能与逆变器业务方面，公司依托“欧洲+新兴市场”双向发力实现营收规模的显着扩张。欧洲市场收入同比增长约59.49%，占总营收比重为59.61%；同时，受当地补贴等储能政策驱动，澳大利亚、越南、菲律宾等新兴市场销售收入分别增长598%、1780%和865%。
尽管储能相关产品销量大幅增长，但受新兴市场价格相对较低、上游原材料涨价及电池产品出口退税率下调等叠加影响，公司当期毛利率降至27.95%，较上年同期减少5.62%。此外，海外业务占比超98%导致的大额汇兑损失也进一步拖累了短期盈利。
下半年，艾罗能源将持续优化产品结构，提升大型储能等新产品的市场占有率，并全面推行精益化管理以推动生产降本增效。
8月24日晚间，科力远披露2026年半年报。上半年，公司实现营业收入24.79亿元，同比增长36.11%；归母净利润5650.36万元，同比增长10.32%；扣非净利润4957.17万元，同比增长4.82%。
公司业绩增长主要源自储能和锂电材料。其中，储能产品实现收入约6.48亿元，较上年同期约1.15亿元增长463.5%，占公司营收比重升至约26%。
制造端，科力远保定储能智能制造产业基地上半年实现储能系统销售1.23GWh，已具备5MWh、6.25MWh储能柜集成能力，远期规划年产能10GWh。与此同时，公司持续通过储能产业基金参与项目投资建设，增强项目获取、投资及运营能力。
项目方面，截至6月底，科力远已推动井陉、望都、谷山梁、诸城、馆陶、罗庄6座独立储能电站并网投运，总装机规模900MW/2600MWh。
目前，科力远已在多个地区储备超过10GWh储能电站项目，下半年计划通过产业基金或其他合作方式投资约4GWh。已投运项目、新增项目和项目储备形成梯次衔接，为后续设备交付和运营资产扩容提供了项目基础。

title: Lancium, Nvidia Partner on Gigawatt-Scale AI Data Centers
content:
Lancium is partnering with Nvidia to deploy the chipmaker’s
AI factory
technology across a portfolio that the Texas-based infrastructure developer says includes 4 GW of leased capacity and more than 15 GW of powered land in development.
The partnership anchors Nvidia’s role in designing and deploying AI infrastructure across Lancium’s portfolio. Lancium will use Nvidia’s DSX reference designs and power-management technologies at its campuses, including systems intended to increase compute density and adjust AI factory power consumption in response to grid conditions.
Nvidia is also making a strategic investment in Lancium, which is backed by Blackstone. The companies did not disclose the investment amount.
Lancium, which calls its data centers “clean campuses,” said its facilities will serve as deployment sites for Nvidia’s full-stack AI factory platform, including accelerated computing, networking and software.
Related:
Data Center Construction at Midyear: Demand, Friction, and Building Discipline
The companies said the arrangement will give cloud providers, infrastructure developers and AI companies in Nvidia’s ecosystem access to power-ready capacity at gigawatt scale.
4 GW vs. 15+ GW
The scale of Lancium’s portfolio is central to the announcement, but its two headline figures represent different stages of development.
The developer says it has 4 GW of capacity under lease and more than 15 GW of powered land under development. The company did not identify the projects behind those figures or provide timelines for bringing the full portfolio online.
Lancium’s publicly announced projects include its
1.2 GW Clean Campus in Abilene
, where Crusoe is developing AI data center capacity as part of the
Stargate project
; a 1 GW campus in Childress County, also with Crusoe; and a new campus near Turkey in Hall County, where QTS will design, build and operate the data center buildings.
Lancium owns the campuses and is responsible for their electrical and civil infrastructure. At the Hall County campus, Lancium and QTS said they will fund all energy infrastructure improvements, with Lancium planning to bring its own power to the site through
battery storage
and solar.
The projects are already attracting billions of dollars in planned investment. QTS and Lancium said the Hall County campus is expected to bring more than $10 billion in capital investment to the region. Lancium also closed a $600 million debt financing package in 2025 to advance its Clean Campus strategy, beginning with the Abilene site.
At Abilene, a 2024 joint venture between Crusoe, Blue Owl Capital, and Primary Digital Infrastructure was established with $3.4 billion to fund more than 200 MW of build-to-suit data center capacity at the Lancium campus.
Related:
Prometheus’ 1.5 GW Texas Data Center Plan Tests Private Power
Those figures are not additive measures of Lancium’s investment. They represent different projects, financing structures and stages of development.
But “powered land” does not necessarily represent load that can be delivered to the grid on the same basis as leased capacity, said Neil Osnato, founder of Persistence Analytics Group.
“Four gigawatts described as ‘under lease’ suggests a materially stronger commercial commitment than 15+ GW of ‘powered land in development,’” Osnato said.
For the larger figure, the important questions are how much capacity an executed interconnection path has, what infrastructure has been studied and is required, when each tranche can energize and how much customer demand is committed behind it, he said.
“A large development pipeline should not automatically be read as 15 GW of executable load,” Osnato said.
Developers are seeking to secure power for AI campuses years before the facilities are fully built. Land, generation resources and an interconnection path can establish a development position without creating an equivalent amount of load that is ready to energize.
Related:
EdgeCore Says Data Centers Should Pay Their Own Power Costs
Grid-Responsive Load
Lancium is also pitching power flexibility as part of the value of its campuses. The company will use Nvidia DSX MaxLPS to improve how power is allocated to GPUs, potentially allowing more GPUs to operate within the same facility power budget, said Matt Kimball, vice president and principal analyst for data center technologies at Moor Insights and Strategy.
The “up to 40%” figure represents an ideal-case scenario rather than a guaranteed improvement, Kimball said. The underlying benefit comes from avoiding the need to reserve each GPU’s maximum rated power when its actual workload typically requires less.
If a GPU is rated at 1 kW but uses 600 watts, for example, conventional power allocation could leave 400 watts of capacity unused. DSX can allocate power based on actual workload requirements, allowing that capacity to be used elsewhere in the facility, he said.
“It’s the ability to better utilize the incoming power” that matters more than the 40% figure, Kimball said.
At a 1 GW facility, even a 20% improvement in power utilization would represent 200 MW of capacity that could potentially support additional GPUs, while a 10% improvement would represent 100 MW, Kimball said. Actual results would depend on workloads and operating conditions.
Kimball said the approach is directionally significant because it connects compute workloads more closely to the data center's available power, rather than treating each GPU’s maximum rated power consumption as a fixed requirement.
For a gigawatt-scale campus, the grid value would depend on what that flexibility can deliver in practice, Osnato said. A useful resource would need to reduce or reshape consumption when the grid needs it, with a response that is fast, measurable, dependable and available during the relevant system conditions.
“The question is not whether the software can technically move load; it is how much load can move, for how long, how often, under whose control, and what operating constraints remain,” he said.
That could affect how utilities
plan for large AI loads
. A genuinely flexible gigawatt-scale customer presents a different planning problem from an inflexible one, Osnato said.
But utilities should not assume that technically available flexibility can substitute for investment in generation or transmission. If a utility relies on a data center’s flexibility to avoid or defer infrastructure, the capability needs to be measurable, available when needed and subject to revalidation as the campus, workload mix and operating economics change.
Lancium said its campuses will combine grid interconnections with behind-the-meter generation and energy storage. Its power-management systems are designed to enable data centers to respond to grid conditions while maintaining the compute density required by AI workloads.
Nvidia’s Role in the Partnership
The Nvidia partnership gives Lancium a technology platform to deploy across its growing data center portfolio, while giving Nvidia customers and infrastructure partners another route to large-scale AI capacity.
“AI factories are the essential infrastructure of this new industrial era,” Nico Caprez, Nvidia’s vice president of global AI infrastructure growth, said in the announcement.
Michael McNamara, Lancium’s CEO and co-founder, said the company had spent years assembling the power, land and infrastructure expertise needed to develop AI data centers at gigawatt scale.
The companies did not disclose which Lancium campuses will use Nvidia technology.
For Lancium, the more consequential test will come as those projects move from development into interconnection and operation.
“Announced capacity is not executable capacity, and technically flexible load is not the same as dependable grid capacity,” Osnato said.
If Lancium can demonstrate both durable load and verifiable flexibility, its model could provide a meaningful grid benefit, he said. The evidence, however, should follow the projects from announcement through interconnection, energization and operation rather than being assumed at the outset.

title: Data Center Construction: Demand, Friction, and Discipline
content:
Data center construction remains the defining infrastructure story of 2026. In a broader construction market showing signs of softness, digital infrastructure is a robust exception. Citing the Dodge Momentum Index,
Construction Dive
reported that data center
construction planning momentum picked up
in July, “again shining as the brightest sector in building.”
This pipeline reflects demand for insurance and risk management expertise in technically complex, capital-intensive projects. Zurich’s global construction insurance business
recorded 18% growth
in the first half of 2026, and since Zurich launched a specialized Data Center Project Guard offering in January, our construction team has received more than three dozen broker submissions representing approximately $140 billion in project value. This is a powerful signal of demand, but demand is not the same as delivery. Friction is increasing, and it is instructive. Friction is a call and an opportunity to innovate, collaborate and communicate.
Related:
Lancium, Nvidia Partner on Gigawatt-Scale AI Data Centers
In the second half of the year, the question is how the technology, construction and insurance industries can deliver on the demand for data center capacity safely, sustainably and with the support of the communities where these projects are slated. The same issues surfaced repeatedly at construction and insurance industry events this summer: power constraints, workforce shortages, insurance capacity, and community concerns chief among them.
Community Concerns Over Data Center Expansion
While energy and labor challenges have been a topic from the start,
community concern
over data centers has heated up this summer.
In July, New York became the first state to
impose a one-year pause
on new hyperscale data centers while the state develops standards intended to protect ratepayers, the energy grid, the environment and local communities. In Texas, Gov. Greg Abbott ordered audits of data center projects seeking grid connection, citing concerns about electricity demand, water use, local impacts, and project transparency.
Dynamics like these are not being dismissed by any of the data center stakeholders in our orbit, whether hyperscalers, co-locators or general contractors. Communities are asking legitimate questions about energy costs, environmental impacts, and long-term accountability.
In the rush to meet the need for digital infrastructure to support advanced AI and society’s growing expectations for financial, healthcare, and entertainment services, these questions must still be addressed. That requires a collaborative approach.
Related:
Prometheus’ 1.5 GW Texas Data Center Plan Tests Private Power
In a recent
Fortune commentary, Chris Crosby
, CEO of Compass Datacenters, made the point that communities need better partners, not blanket bans, and that trust must be earned through transparency, regular communication and commitments residents can see over time. He outlined five questions that every data center developer should address for the community. That is a constructive way to frame the challenge.
Balancing Growth and Community Expectations
That broader perspective is increasingly important as campuses grow larger and more complex, driven by the need for more computing power in one place to improve AI training and inference performance.
When engaged early, insurance underwriting and risk engineering teams can help surface issues before they become costly problems. Early plan review can help owners address protection systems and engineering requirements up front to support longer-term insurability. Resolving these matters earlier can be pivotal to securing ongoing property insurance on terms and at pricing the owner would prefer.
Related:
EdgeCore Says Data Centers Should Pay Their Own Power Costs
Collaborative Solutions
Power specialists in our risk engineering group point out that the discussion on energy sourcing is rapidly evolving. It’s no longer only about whether enough electricity can be generated from the grid for the data center. It is about whether high-quality, reliable power can be delivered when it is needed to all who depend on it, including homes and businesses.
Data center developers are evaluating multiple pathways to alleviate strain on the electrical grid, including natural gas microgrids, fuel cells, battery energy storage systems, geothermal and, over a longer time horizon, nuclear. Many are committed to paying for their additional usage in one way or another.
We are still a long way from fit-out, as the industry navigates the challenges of this unprecedented buildout to support the AI revolution. But foundations are being laid. The data center buildout has only just begun, but is already entering a more disciplined, collaborative phase.
